questions.subject: science
questions.q: What is the SI unit of luminous intensity?
questions.explanation: The candela (cd) is the SI base unit of luminous intensity.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: What is the dimensional formula of force?
questions.explanation: Force = mass × acceleration = M × LT⁻², so its dimensions are MLT⁻².

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Which of the following is a derived quantity and not a base quantity in the SI system?
questions.explanation: Length, time and mass are base quantities; force is derived from them (kg m s⁻²).

questions.subject: science
questions.q: How many significant figures does the measurement 0.04050 m have?
questions.explanation: Leading zeros are not significant, while the final zero after the decimal point is; the significant digits are 4, 0, 5, 0.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: A physical quantity has dimensions ML²T⁻³. Which quantity is it?
questions.explanation: Power = energy/time = ML²T⁻²/T = ML²T⁻³.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Distinguish between the accuracy and the precision of a measurement.
questions.answer: Accuracy is how close a measured value is to the true value. Precision is how close repeated measurements are to one another, whatever the true value is.
keyPoints: Accuracy: closeness to the true value
Precision: closeness of repeated readings to each other
A measurement can be precise but not accurate
questions.explanation: Precision describes the spread of readings; accuracy describes the error relative to the true value.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: The quantity √(P/ρ), where P is pressure and ρ is density, has the same dimensions as which of the following?
questions.explanation: P/ρ = ML⁻¹T⁻² / ML⁻³ = L²T⁻², whose square root is LT⁻¹, the dimension of velocity.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Why can dimensional analysis not give the numerical constant in a formula such as s = ½at²?
questions.answer: Pure numbers such as ½ are dimensionless, so they do not affect whether the dimensions of two sides match. Dimensional analysis can check the form of a relation but cannot fix such constants.
keyPoints: Dimensions match whatever the constant is
The constant must be found by experiment or derivation
questions.explanation: Dimensional checks are blind to dimensionless factors, so they only test the structure of an equation.

questions.subject: science
questions.topic: Motion in a Straight Line and in a Plane
questions.q: The slope of a position-time graph of a moving body gives its:
questions.explanation: Slope = change in position / change in time, which is velocity.

questions.subject: science
questions.topic: Motion in a Straight Line and in a Plane
questions.q: Which of the following is a vector quantity?
questions.explanation: Velocity has both magnitude and direction; speed, distance and mass are scalars.

questions.subject: science
questions.topic: Motion in a Straight Line and in a Plane
questions.q: A body moves in uniform circular motion. Which quantity stays constant?
questions.explanation: The direction of velocity and acceleration keeps changing, but the magnitude of velocity (speed) stays constant.

questions.subject: science
questions.topic: Motion in a Straight Line and in a Plane
questions.q: A car starts from rest and moves with a uniform acceleration of 2 m/s² for 10 s. How far does it travel?
questions.explanation: s = ut + ½at² = 0 + ½ × 2 × 10² = 100 m.

questions.subject: science
questions.topic: Motion in a Straight Line and in a Plane
questions.q: A ball is thrown vertically upward with a speed of 20 m/s. Taking g = 10 m/s² and ignoring air resistance, what is the maximum height reached?

questions.subject: science
questions.topic: Motion in a Straight Line and in a Plane
questions.q: Two trains move in the same direction on parallel tracks at 60 km/h and 45 km/h. Find the velocity of the faster train relative to the slower one.
questions.answer: Relative velocity = 60 − 45 = 15 km/h, in the direction of motion.
keyPoints: Same direction, so subtract the velocities
questions.explanation: For motion along one line in the same direction, v(AB) = vA − vB.

questions.subject: science
questions.topic: Motion in a Straight Line and in a Plane
questions.q: Two projectiles are launched from level ground with the same speed, one at 30° and the other at 60° to the horizontal. Ignoring air resistance, how do their horizontal ranges compare?
options: It cannot be decided without the speed
questions.explanation: Range R = u² sin2θ / g, and sin 60° = sin 120°, so angles that add up to 90° give equal ranges.

questions.subject: science
questions.topic: Motion in a Straight Line and in a Plane
questions.q: What are the velocity and the acceleration of a projectile at the highest point of its path (ignoring air resistance)?
questions.answer: The velocity is not zero: only its vertical component is zero, so the projectile moves horizontally with speed u cosθ. The acceleration is still g, directed downward.
keyPoints: Vertical velocity component is zero at the top
Horizontal component u cosθ stays constant
questions.explanation: Gravity acts throughout the flight and there is no horizontal force, so horizontal velocity is unchanged.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: What is the SI unit of force?
questions.explanation: The newton (N) equals 1 kg m s⁻².

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Newton's first law of motion is also known as the law of:
questions.explanation: The first law states that a body keeps its state of rest or uniform motion unless acted on by a net force, which is inertia.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: According to Newton's second law, the net force on a body of mass m with acceleration a is:
questions.explanation: F = ma is the standard statement of the second law for constant mass.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: What net force gives a 5 kg mass an acceleration of 3 m/s²?

questions.subject: science
questions.q: A 0.15 kg ball moving at 20 m/s is brought to rest by a fielder in 0.1 s. What average force does the hand exert?
questions.explanation: F = change in momentum / time = 0.15 × 20 / 0.1 = 30 N.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Why do passengers in a moving bus lurch forward when the driver applies the brakes suddenly?
questions.answer: The bus slows down, but the passengers' bodies tend to keep moving at the earlier speed because of inertia, so they appear to be thrown forward.
keyPoints: Bus stops but the body tends to continue moving
No force pushes the passenger forward
questions.explanation: This is Newton's first law: a body continues in its state of motion unless a force changes it.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: A 2 kg block rests on a rough horizontal table (coefficient of static friction 0.5, g = 10 m/s²). A horizontal force of 8 N is applied to it. What is the force of friction on the block?
questions.explanation: Maximum static friction is 0.5 × 2 × 10 = 10 N. The applied 8 N is less than this, so the block stays at rest and friction exactly balances it at 8 N.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: A gun of mass 4 kg fires a bullet of mass 20 g at 200 m/s. Find the recoil speed of the gun.
questions.answer: By conservation of momentum, 4 × V = 0.02 × 200, so V = 1 m/s, in the direction opposite to the bullet.
keyPoints: Total momentum before firing is zero
mass of gun × V = mass of bullet × v
Recoil speed is 1 m/s, opposite to the bullet
questions.explanation: 0.02 kg × 200 m/s = 4 kg m/s, divided by 4 kg gives 1 m/s.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: What is the SI unit of work?
questions.explanation: Work is measured in joules (J), where 1 J = 1 N m.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: The work done by a force that acts perpendicular to the displacement of a body is:
questions.explanation: W = Fs cosθ, and cos 90° = 0.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: The kinetic energy of a body of mass m moving with speed v is:
questions.explanation: Kinetic energy is given by ½mv².

questions.subject: science
questions.q: What is the kinetic energy of a 2 kg body moving at 3 m/s?

questions.subject: science
questions.q: A 60 W bulb is used for 5 hours. How much electrical energy does it consume?
questions.explanation: Energy = 0.06 kW × 5 h = 0.3 kWh.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Calculate the work done against gravity in lifting a 10 kg load through a height of 5 m. Take g = 10 m/s².
questions.explanation: The work done equals the gain in gravitational potential energy.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: If the momentum of a body is doubled (its mass staying the same), by what percentage does its kinetic energy increase?
questions.explanation: KE = p²/2m. Doubling p makes KE four times the original, which is an increase of 300%.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: A car is braked with the same constant braking force at speed v and then at speed 2v. Compare the stopping distances and explain.
questions.answer: The stopping distance at 2v is four times that at v. The work done by the brakes, F × d, must equal the kinetic energy ½mv², so d is proportional to v².
keyPoints: Work done by brakes = initial kinetic energy
F d = ½mv², so d ∝ v²
Doubling the speed gives four times the distance
questions.explanation: Kinetic energy depends on the square of speed.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Who formulated the law of universal gravitation?
questions.explanation: Isaac Newton proposed that every two masses attract each other with a force along the line joining them.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: What is the SI unit of the universal gravitational constant G?
questions.explanation: From F = Gm₁m₂/r², G = Fr²/(m₁m₂), whose unit is N m² kg⁻².

questions.subject: science
questions.q: The acceleration due to gravity near the Earth's surface is approximately:
questions.explanation: The standard value of g near the Earth's surface is about 9.8 m/s².

questions.subject: science
questions.q: At a height equal to the Earth's radius above the surface, the acceleration due to gravity is (g = value at the surface):
questions.explanation: The distance from the centre is 2R, so g' = g (R/2R)² = g/4.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: The escape velocity from the surface of the Earth is approximately:
questions.explanation: The escape velocity from Earth is √(2gR), about 11.2 km/s.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Distinguish between G and g.
questions.answer: G is the universal gravitational constant, the same everywhere (6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻²). g is the acceleration due to gravity of a particular planet, which varies with place, height and depth (about 9.8 m/s² on Earth).
keyPoints: g depends on the planet and on location
questions.explanation: g can be written in terms of G, the planet's mass M and its radius R.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: An astronaut whose mass is 70 kg on Earth lands on the Moon, where g is about one-sixth of the Earth's. Which statement is correct?
options: Her mass stays 70 kg and her weight becomes about one-sixth
Her mass becomes 420 kg and her weight is unchanged
Both her mass and weight are unchanged
questions.explanation: Mass is the amount of matter and does not change with place; weight = mg depends on g.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Why do astronauts in an orbiting satellite feel weightless even though gravity still acts on them?
questions.answer: The astronaut and the satellite are both in free fall around the Earth with the same acceleration, so there is no contact force between them. Gravity provides the centripetal force, and the apparent weight is zero.
keyPoints: Satellite and astronaut fall together with the same acceleration
Gravity is still acting and supplies centripetal force
No normal reaction, so apparent weight is zero
questions.explanation: Weightlessness means zero apparent weight, not zero gravity.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: The number of particles in one mole of a substance is:
questions.explanation: One mole contains Avogadro's number, 6.022 × 10²³, of particles.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Which scientist stated the law of conservation of mass for chemical reactions?
questions.explanation: Antoine Lavoisier showed that mass is neither created nor destroyed in a chemical reaction.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: What is the molar mass of water (H₂O)? (H = 1, O = 16)

questions.subject: science
questions.q: What is the mass of 2 moles of carbon dioxide, CO₂? (C = 12, O = 16)
questions.explanation: Molar mass of CO₂ = 44 g/mol, so 2 mol = 88 g.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: How many molecules are present in 4.4 g of CO₂? (Molar mass 44 g/mol; Avogadro number 6.022 × 10²³)
questions.explanation: 4.4 g is 0.1 mol, and 0.1 × 6.022 × 10²³ = 6.022 × 10²² molecules.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Calculate the molarity of a solution made by dissolving 4 g of NaOH in water and making the volume 500 mL. (Na = 23, O = 16, H = 1)
questions.answer: Moles of NaOH = 4/40 = 0.1 mol. Volume = 0.5 L. Molarity = 0.1/0.5 = 0.2 M.
keyPoints: Molar mass of NaOH is 40 g/mol
questions.explanation: Molarity = moles of solute / volume of solution in litres.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: In the reaction 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O, 2 mol of H₂ is mixed with 2 mol of O₂ and the reaction goes to completion. How many moles of water are formed?
questions.explanation: 2 mol of H₂ needs only 1 mol of O₂, so H₂ is the limiting reagent and gives 2 mol of H₂O.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: A compound contains 40% carbon, 6.7% hydrogen and 53.3% oxygen by mass. Find its empirical formula. (C = 12, H = 1, O = 16)
questions.answer: Moles: C = 40/12 = 3.33, H = 6.7/1 = 6.7, O = 53.3/16 = 3.33. Dividing by 3.33 gives the ratio 1 : 2 : 1, so the empirical formula is CH₂O.
keyPoints: Ratio C : H : O = 1 : 2 : 1, so CH₂O
questions.explanation: The empirical formula is the simplest whole-number ratio of atoms.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Who discovered the electron?
questions.explanation: J. J. Thomson discovered the electron through cathode-ray experiments.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: The neutron was discovered by:
questions.explanation: James Chadwick discovered the neutron in 1932.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: The atomic number of an element is equal to the number of:
questions.explanation: Atomic number Z is defined as the number of protons in the nucleus.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: How many neutrons are present in an atom of sodium-23 (atomic number 11)?
questions.explanation: Neutrons = mass number − atomic number = 23 − 11 = 12.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: What is the maximum number of electrons that the third shell (n = 3) can hold?
questions.explanation: The maximum is 2n² = 2 × 9 = 18.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Write the electronic configuration of chlorine (atomic number 17) in terms of subshells.
keyPoints: Seven electrons in the outer shell
questions.explanation: 2 + 2 + 6 + 2 + 5 = 17 electrons.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Which set of quantum numbers (n, l, m) is NOT permissible for an electron in an atom?
questions.explanation: For a given n, l can only take values from 0 to n − 1, so l = 2 is not allowed when n = 2.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: In Rutherford's alpha-particle scattering experiment, what did each of the three observations show about the atom?
questions.answer: Most particles passed straight through, so most of the atom is empty space. A few were deflected through large angles, so there is a small, positively charged centre. A very few bounced back, so the nucleus is very dense and holds most of the mass.
keyPoints: Most pass through: atom is mostly empty space
Some deflected: positive nucleus repels alpha particles
Very few rebound: nucleus is small and dense
questions.explanation: These observations led to the nuclear model of the atom.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: According to the modern periodic law, the properties of elements are a periodic function of their:
questions.explanation: Moseley's work led to arranging elements by atomic number rather than atomic mass.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: How many groups are there in the modern (long form) periodic table?
questions.explanation: The long form periodic table has 18 vertical groups and 7 periods.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: The halogens belong to which group of the periodic table?
questions.explanation: Fluorine, chlorine, bromine, iodine and astatine form Group 17.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Among the alkali metals Li, Na, K and Rb, which has the largest atomic radius?
questions.explanation: Atomic radius increases down a group because of the addition of electron shells; Rb is the lowest of the four.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Which of these elements has the highest electronegativity?
questions.explanation: Fluorine is the most electronegative element.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Define ionisation enthalpy and state how it generally changes across a period from left to right.
questions.answer: Ionisation enthalpy is the energy required to remove the most loosely held electron from an isolated gaseous atom. It generally increases across a period because the nuclear charge rises and the atomic size decreases.
keyPoints: Energy to remove outermost electron from a gaseous atom
Increases from left to right in a period
Because of greater nuclear charge and smaller radius
questions.explanation: A stronger pull from the nucleus makes the electron harder to remove.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: The species O²⁻, F⁻, Na⁺ and Mg²⁺ all have the same number of electrons. Which has the largest radius?
questions.explanation: With the same number of electrons, the species with the fewest protons (O²⁻, 8) has the weakest nuclear pull and is largest.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Why is the first ionisation enthalpy of beryllium greater than that of boron even though boron has the higher atomic number?
questions.answer: Beryllium's outer electron is in a filled 2s orbital, which is relatively stable and held tightly. Boron's outer electron is in the 2p orbital, which is higher in energy and partly shielded by the 2s electrons, so it is easier to remove.
keyPoints: B's electron to be removed is in 2p
2p electron is at higher energy and shielded, so removed more easily
questions.explanation: This is an exception to the general rise in ionisation enthalpy across a period.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: A bond formed by the complete transfer of electrons from one atom to another is called:
questions.explanation: Transfer of electrons gives oppositely charged ions held together by electrostatic attraction, an ionic bond.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: What is the shape of a methane (CH₄) molecule?
questions.explanation: Carbon is sp³ hybridised with four bond pairs, giving a tetrahedral shape.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: How many bonds join the two nitrogen atoms in an N₂ molecule?
questions.explanation: Each N atom needs three more electrons to complete an octet, so they share three pairs: a triple bond.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: What is the hybridisation of each carbon atom in ethene, C₂H₄?
questions.explanation: Each carbon forms three sigma bonds (two C–H and one C–C), which corresponds to sp² hybridisation.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: The H–O–H bond angle in a water molecule is about:
questions.explanation: Two lone pairs on oxygen repel the bond pairs and reduce the angle below 109.5° to about 104.5°.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Solid sodium chloride does not conduct electricity, but molten sodium chloride does. Explain why.
questions.answer: In the solid the Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions are held in fixed positions in the lattice, so no charge can move. When molten, the ions are free to move and carry current.
keyPoints: Ions are fixed in the solid lattice
Ions are mobile in the molten state
questions.explanation: Conduction in ionic compounds needs mobile ions.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Which of the following molecules is linear?
questions.explanation: In CO₂ the carbon atom is sp hybridised with no lone pairs, so the molecule is linear (O=C=O).

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Water boils at a much higher temperature than hydrogen sulphide (H₂S), though H₂S has a larger molar mass. Explain.
questions.answer: Oxygen is highly electronegative, so water molecules form strong hydrogen bonds with one another. These need extra energy to break. H₂S molecules do not form significant hydrogen bonds, so they separate more easily.
keyPoints: Oxygen is much more electronegative than sulphur
H₂S has only weak forces, so lower boiling point
questions.explanation: Intermolecular hydrogen bonding outweighs the effect of molar mass here.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Who first used the term 'cell' after observing a thin slice of cork?
questions.explanation: Robert Hooke observed cork under a microscope in 1665 and named the small compartments cells.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Which cell organelle is called the powerhouse of the cell?
questions.explanation: Mitochondria produce most of the cell's ATP by respiration.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Which of these organisms has cells without a true nucleus?
questions.explanation: Bacteria are prokaryotes, whose genetic material is not enclosed by a nuclear membrane.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Protein synthesis takes place at:
questions.explanation: Ribosomes translate mRNA into polypeptide chains.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: The main chemical component of the cell wall of plants is:
questions.explanation: Plant cell walls are made chiefly of cellulose; chitin occurs in fungi and peptidoglycan in bacteria.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: State two differences between a prokaryotic cell and a eukaryotic cell.
questions.answer: A prokaryotic cell has no membrane-bound nucleus (the DNA lies free in the nucleoid) and lacks membrane-bound organelles such as mitochondria. A eukaryotic cell has a true nucleus and membrane-bound organelles.
keyPoints: Prokaryote: no nuclear membrane, eukaryote: true nucleus
questions.explanation: These structural differences separate bacteria from plants, animals and fungi.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: A chemical destroys all the lysosomes of a cell. What is the most likely result?
options: The cell can no longer make proteins
The cell loses its cell wall
Worn-out organelles and engulfed material accumulate undigested
The cell cannot divide at all
questions.explanation: Lysosomes contain hydrolytic enzymes that digest worn-out organelles and ingested material.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Why do muscle cells contain a much larger number of mitochondria than skin cells?
questions.answer: Muscle cells contract continuously and need a large and steady supply of ATP. Mitochondria produce ATP by aerobic respiration, so more mitochondria meet this high energy demand.
keyPoints: Muscle cells have high energy demand
More mitochondria means more ATP production
questions.explanation: The number of an organelle usually matches the function of the cell.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: The building blocks (monomers) of proteins are:
questions.explanation: Proteins are polymers of amino acids joined by peptide bonds.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: The bond that joins two amino acids in a protein is called a:
questions.explanation: A peptide bond forms between the carboxyl group of one amino acid and the amino group of the next.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Which of the following is a polysaccharide?
questions.explanation: Starch is a polymer of glucose; glucose and fructose are monosaccharides and sucrose is a disaccharide.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Most enzymes are chemically:
questions.explanation: The great majority of enzymes are globular proteins.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Which nitrogenous base is present in RNA but not in DNA?
questions.explanation: RNA contains uracil in place of the thymine found in DNA.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: What is the active site of an enzyme, and what role does it play?
questions.answer: The active site is a specific region on the enzyme surface with a shape and chemistry that fit the substrate. The substrate binds there and is converted into product.
keyPoints: Substrate binds and is converted to product
questions.explanation: The fit of the substrate to the active site explains the specificity of enzymes.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: An enzyme solution is heated to 90 °C and loses its activity, which does not return when it is cooled. The best explanation is that:
options: the substrate has been used up
the enzyme's three-dimensional structure has been permanently denatured
questions.explanation: High temperature breaks the weak bonds holding the folded shape, so the active site is lost permanently.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Why are animal fats, rich in saturated fatty acids, usually solid at room temperature while plant oils, rich in unsaturated fatty acids, are liquid?
questions.answer: Saturated fatty acid chains are straight and pack closely, so the molecules attract each other strongly and the fat is solid. Unsaturated chains have double bonds that bend the chain, so they pack loosely and the oil stays liquid.
keyPoints: Saturated chains are straight and pack closely
Double bonds in unsaturated chains cause kinks
Looser packing means a lower melting point
questions.explanation: Melting point depends on how tightly the molecules can pack.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Which is the main pigment that directly takes part in photosynthesis?
questions.explanation: Chlorophyll a is the main photosynthetic pigment; the others are accessory or non-photosynthetic pigments.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: The light-dependent reactions of photosynthesis take place in the:
questions.explanation: The pigments and electron carriers for the light reactions lie in the thylakoid (grana) membranes.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Glycolysis, the first step of respiration, takes place in the:
questions.explanation: Glycolysis occurs in the cytoplasm and does not need oxygen.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: What is the net gain of ATP from glycolysis of one glucose molecule?
questions.explanation: Glycolysis uses 2 ATP and makes 4 ATP, a net gain of 2.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: The oxygen released during photosynthesis comes from:
questions.explanation: Photolysis of water splits H₂O, releasing O₂.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Write the overall balanced equation for photosynthesis and name the two requirements other than the reactants.
questions.answer: 6CO₂ + 12H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ + 6H₂O, in the presence of light and chlorophyll.
questions.explanation: The equation can also be written with 6H₂O on each side cancelled: 6CO₂ + 6H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Why does the Calvin cycle stop after a short time if a plant is moved into darkness, even though CO₂ is available?
options: The ATP and NADPH made in the light reactions are used up
CO₂ cannot enter the chloroplast in the dark
questions.explanation: The Calvin cycle uses ATP and NADPH from the light reactions; without light they are not regenerated.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Compare aerobic respiration with fermentation in terms of end products and energy released.
questions.answer: Aerobic respiration oxidises glucose completely to CO₂ and H₂O and releases a large amount of energy (about 30 to 38 ATP per glucose). Fermentation gives incomplete breakdown into ethanol and CO₂ (or lactic acid) and releases only 2 ATP.
keyPoints: Aerobic: CO₂ and water, many ATP
Fermentation: ethanol and CO₂ or lactic acid
questions.explanation: Complete oxidation extracts much more of the energy stored in glucose.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Which muscular structure separates the thoracic cavity from the abdominal cavity in humans?
questions.explanation: The diaphragm lies below the lungs and plays a major role in breathing.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Which respiratory pigment carries most of the oxygen in human blood?
questions.explanation: Haemoglobin in red blood cells binds oxygen to carry it from the lungs to tissues.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Blood vessels that carry blood away from the heart are called:
questions.explanation: Arteries carry blood away from the heart; veins bring blood back to it.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: The normal blood pressure of a healthy adult human is approximately:
questions.explanation: Normal blood pressure is about 120 mm Hg systolic and 80 mm Hg diastolic.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Which chamber of the human heart receives oxygenated blood from the lungs?
questions.explanation: Pulmonary veins bring oxygenated blood from the lungs to the left atrium.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: How is carbon dioxide transported in the blood?
questions.answer: About 70% is carried as bicarbonate ions in the plasma, about 20 to 25% is bound to haemoglobin as carbamino-haemoglobin, and about 7% is dissolved in plasma.
questions.explanation: Carbonic anhydrase in red blood cells speeds up the formation of bicarbonate.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: People who go to high altitudes tend to breathe faster at first. What is the main reason?
options: The air there contains more carbon dioxide
The lower partial pressure of oxygen means less oxygen reaches the blood
questions.explanation: At altitude the partial pressure of oxygen is lower, so the blood takes up less oxygen and breathing rate increases to compensate.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Why is the wall of the left ventricle thicker than that of the right ventricle?
questions.answer: The left ventricle pumps blood at high pressure to the whole body through the aorta, whereas the right ventricle pumps blood only to the nearby lungs at lower pressure. A thicker muscular wall generates the greater force needed.
keyPoints: Left ventricle supplies the whole body
Right ventricle supplies only the lungs
questions.explanation: Wall thickness matches the pressure the chamber must generate.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: What is the SI unit of pressure?
questions.explanation: Pressure is force per unit area, and its SI unit is the pascal (1 Pa = 1 N/m²).

questions.subject: science
questions.q: State the SI base units of length, mass and time.
questions.answer: Length is measured in metre (m), mass in kilogram (kg) and time in second (s).
questions.explanation: These are three of the seven SI base units.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: What is the dimensional formula of pressure?
questions.explanation: Pressure = force / area = MLT⁻² / L² = ML⁻¹T⁻².

questions.subject: science
questions.q: The number 3.14159 is rounded off to three significant figures. The result is:
questions.explanation: The fourth digit is 1, which is less than 5, so the third significant figure stays unchanged: 3.14.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Which pair of quantities has the same dimensions?
questions.explanation: Both work and torque have dimensions ML²T⁻²; the other pairs differ.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Two lengths, 2.5 cm and 3.25 cm, are measured with different instruments and added. Using the rule for adding measurements, the result should be reported as:
questions.explanation: The sum 5.75 cm can only be as precise as the least precise value (one decimal place), so it is rounded to 5.8 cm.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: The radius of a sphere is measured with a possible error of 2%. What is the possible percentage error in its calculated volume?
questions.explanation: Volume is proportional to r³, so the fractional errors add three times: 3 × 2% = 6%.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: The time period of a simple pendulum is T = 2π√(l/g). If the length l is measured with a 1% error, what is the resulting percentage error in T (g taken as exact)?
questions.answer: T is proportional to l to the power ½, so the percentage error in T is ½ × 1% = 0.5%.
keyPoints: T is proportional to the square root of l
Error is multiplied by the power ½
questions.explanation: For a quantity raised to power n, the percentage error is n times that of the base.

questions.subject: science
questions.topic: Motion in a Straight Line and in a Plane
questions.q: Which of the following is the SI unit of acceleration?
questions.explanation: Acceleration is change in velocity per unit time, so its unit is m/s².

questions.subject: science
questions.topic: Motion in a Straight Line and in a Plane
questions.q: Differentiate between distance and displacement.
questions.answer: Distance is the total length of the path travelled and is a scalar. Displacement is the shortest straight-line change in position from start to end, with direction, and is a vector.
keyPoints: Displacement: change in position with direction, vector
Distance is never less than the magnitude of displacement
questions.explanation: A body returning to its starting point has zero displacement but non-zero distance.

questions.subject: science
questions.topic: Motion in a Straight Line and in a Plane
questions.q: A person walks 3 m east and then 4 m north. What is the magnitude of the displacement from the starting point?
questions.explanation: The displacement is the hypotenuse of a 3-4-5 right triangle, so 5 m.

questions.subject: science
questions.topic: Motion in a Straight Line and in a Plane
questions.q: A car is moving at 72 km/h. What is its speed in m/s?

questions.subject: science
questions.topic: Motion in a Straight Line and in a Plane
questions.q: A stone is dropped from rest. Taking g = 10 m/s² and ignoring air resistance, how far does it fall in the first 2 seconds?

questions.subject: science
questions.topic: Motion in a Straight Line and in a Plane
questions.q: The velocity of a body increases uniformly from 0 to 8 m/s in 4 s. What distance does it cover in this time?
questions.explanation: The distance is the area under the velocity-time graph: ½ × 4 × 8 = 16 m.

questions.subject: science
questions.topic: Motion in a Straight Line and in a Plane
questions.q: Rain falls vertically at 10 m/s. A man walks on level ground at 10 m/s. At what angle to the vertical must he tilt his umbrella to keep dry?
questions.explanation: The rain relative to the man has equal vertical and horizontal components of 10 m/s, so tan θ = 1 and θ = 45°, tilted forward.

questions.subject: science
questions.topic: Motion in a Straight Line and in a Plane
questions.q: A ball is thrown from level ground at 45° to the horizontal with a speed of 20 m/s. Taking g = 10 m/s², find its horizontal range.
questions.explanation: A launch angle of 45° gives the maximum range for a given speed.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Which statement is Newton's third law of motion?
options: To every action there is an equal and opposite reaction
A body at rest stays at rest unless a net force acts on it
Force is the rate of change of velocity
questions.explanation: The third law says forces between two bodies are equal in magnitude and opposite in direction.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Define linear momentum and state its SI unit.
questions.answer: Linear momentum is the product of the mass and the velocity of a body, p = mv. Its SI unit is kg m/s.
keyPoints: It is a vector in the direction of velocity
questions.explanation: Newton's second law can be written as force = rate of change of momentum.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: What is the momentum of a 2 kg ball moving at 5 m/s?
questions.explanation: p = mv = 2 × 5 = 10 kg m/s.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Which type of friction is generally the smallest for a given pair of surfaces and load?
questions.explanation: Rolling friction is much smaller than sliding or limiting static friction, which is why wheels are used.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: The impulse of a force acting on a body is equal to the:
options: product of its mass and velocity
questions.explanation: Impulse = force × time = change in momentum.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: A 60 kg person stands on a weighing scale in a lift that is accelerating upward at 2 m/s². Taking g = 10 m/s², what force does the scale exert on the person?
questions.explanation: N − mg = ma, so N = m(g + a) = 60 × 12 = 720 N.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Masses of 3 kg and 5 kg hang from the two ends of a light string passing over a smooth pulley. Taking g = 10 m/s², what is the acceleration of the masses?

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Why does a cricketer move his hands backward while catching a fast cricket ball?
questions.answer: Moving the hands back increases the time over which the ball's momentum is brought to zero. The change in momentum is fixed, so a longer time means a smaller average force on the hands.
keyPoints: Longer time gives a smaller force and avoids injury
questions.explanation: This uses the impulse-momentum relation F × Δt = Δp.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: What is the SI unit of power?
questions.explanation: Power is the rate of doing work and is measured in watts (1 W = 1 J/s).

questions.subject: science
questions.q: State the work-energy theorem.
questions.answer: The net work done on a body by all the forces acting on it is equal to the change in its kinetic energy.
keyPoints: Net work done equals change in kinetic energy
questions.explanation: It links the work done by forces to the change in the speed of a body.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: What is the gravitational potential energy of a 2 kg body at a height of 20 m above the ground? Take g = 10 m/s².

questions.subject: science
questions.q: One kilowatt-hour is equal to:

questions.subject: science
questions.q: A pump raises 100 kg of water through a height of 10 m in 10 s. Taking g = 10 m/s², the power used is:

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Two bodies collide and stick together (a perfectly inelastic collision). Which of the following is conserved?
questions.explanation: Momentum is conserved in every collision with no external force, but some kinetic energy is converted to other forms in an inelastic collision.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: A ball is dropped from a height of 20 m. Ignoring air resistance and taking g = 10 m/s², its speed just before hitting the ground is:
questions.explanation: By energy conservation, ½mv² = mgh, so v = √(2gh) = √400 = 20 m/s.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: A spring of force constant 200 N/m is compressed by 0.1 m. How much energy is stored in it? If it is released to push a 0.5 kg block on a smooth horizontal surface, what is the block's speed on leaving the spring?
questions.answer: Energy stored = ½kx² = ½ × 200 × 0.01 = 1 J. This becomes kinetic energy, ½ × 0.5 × v² = 1, so v = 2 m/s.
keyPoints: All of it becomes kinetic energy
questions.explanation: No energy is lost on a smooth surface.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Kepler's law of periods states that the square of the time period of a planet is proportional to the cube of its:
questions.explanation: T² is proportional to a³, where a is the semi-major axis of the planet's orbit.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: State Kepler's law of areas.
questions.answer: The line joining a planet to the Sun sweeps out equal areas in equal intervals of time. So the planet moves faster when it is closer to the Sun.
keyPoints: Planet moves faster when nearer the Sun
questions.explanation: This is a consequence of conservation of angular momentum.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: The orbit of a planet around the Sun is:
options: an ellipse with the Sun at one focus
a perfect circle with the Sun at the centre
questions.explanation: Kepler's first law states that planets move in elliptical orbits with the Sun at one focus.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: What is the approximate gravitational force between two 1 kg masses placed 1 m apart? (G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻²)

questions.subject: science
questions.q: If the distance between two masses is doubled, the gravitational force between them becomes:
questions.explanation: Force varies as 1/r², so doubling r reduces the force to one-fourth.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: As one moves from the equator towards the poles on the Earth's surface, the value of g:
questions.explanation: The Earth is slightly flattened, so the poles are closer to the centre, and the effect of rotation is absent at the poles; both make g larger there.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Taking g = 9.8 m/s² and the Earth's radius as 6.4 × 10⁶ m, the orbital speed of a satellite revolving very close to the Earth's surface is approximately:

questions.subject: science
questions.q: State three features of a geostationary satellite and explain why it appears fixed in the sky.
questions.answer: It orbits in the equatorial plane, from west to east, with a period of 24 hours, at a height of about 36,000 km. Because it takes the same time as the Earth to complete one rotation, it stays above the same point on the Earth.
keyPoints: Orbits in the equatorial plane, west to east
Same angular speed as the Earth so it appears stationary
questions.explanation: Such satellites are used for communication and broadcasting.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: The law of definite proportions was put forward by:
questions.explanation: Joseph Proust showed that a given compound always has the same elements combined in the same proportion by mass.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Differentiate between an atom and a molecule.
questions.answer: An atom is the smallest particle of an element that takes part in a chemical reaction. A molecule is a group of two or more atoms, of the same or different elements, bonded together and able to exist independently.
keyPoints: Atom: smallest unit of an element
Molecule: two or more atoms bonded together
Example: H is an atom, H₂ is a molecule
questions.explanation: Elements such as H₂ and O₂ exist as molecules of identical atoms.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: How many moles of water are present in 36 g of water? (H = 1, O = 16)

questions.subject: science
questions.q: How many oxygen atoms are present in 0.5 mol of O₂ gas? (N_A = 6.022 × 10²³)
questions.explanation: 0.5 mol of O₂ has 0.5 × 6.022 × 10²³ molecules, each with 2 atoms: 6.022 × 10²³ atoms.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: What is the mass percentage of carbon in carbon dioxide? (C = 12, O = 16)

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Propane burns completely as C₃H₈ + 5O₂ → 3CO₂ + 4H₂O. How many moles of oxygen are needed to burn 1 mol of propane completely?
questions.explanation: The balanced equation shows that 1 mol of propane reacts with 5 mol of oxygen.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Which of the following concentration terms does not change when the temperature of a solution changes?
questions.explanation: Molality is moles of solute per kilogram of solvent. Mass does not change with temperature, whereas volume does.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: 10 g of calcium carbonate is heated strongly: CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂. Calculate the mass of CaO and of CO₂ formed. (Ca = 40, C = 12, O = 16)
questions.answer: Moles of CaCO₃ = 10/100 = 0.1 mol. This gives 0.1 mol CaO = 0.1 × 56 = 5.6 g and 0.1 mol CO₂ = 0.1 × 44 = 4.4 g. The total, 10 g, equals the mass of the reactant.
keyPoints: CO₂ = 4.4 g, and the masses add up to 10 g
questions.explanation: This verifies the law of conservation of mass.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: What is the charge on a proton?
questions.explanation: A proton carries a charge equal in size to an electron's but positive.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: What are isotopes? Give one example.
questions.answer: Isotopes are atoms of the same element with the same atomic number but different mass numbers, because they have different numbers of neutrons. Example: protium, deuterium and tritium of hydrogen.
questions.explanation: Isotopes have almost identical chemical properties.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: How many electrons are present in an Fe³⁺ ion? (Atomic number of Fe = 26)
questions.explanation: Fe³⁺ has lost three electrons, so 26 − 3 = 23.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: According to the Aufbau principle, which subshell is filled immediately after 3p?
questions.explanation: The 4s subshell has lower energy than 3d, so it is filled before 3d.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: According to the Pauli exclusion principle, the maximum number of electrons in one orbital is:
questions.explanation: An orbital can hold at most two electrons, which must have opposite spins.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: How many unpaired electrons are there in a nitrogen atom (1s² 2s² 2p³) in its ground state?
questions.explanation: By Hund's rule, the three 2p electrons occupy separate p orbitals with parallel spins, so all three are unpaired.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Which photon has more energy: one of wavelength 400 nm or one of wavelength 700 nm?
options: It depends on the intensity of the light
questions.explanation: E = hc/λ, so the shorter wavelength gives the higher photon energy.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Calculate the energy of a photon of light of frequency 5 × 10¹⁴ Hz. (h = 6.626 × 10⁻³⁴ J s)
questions.explanation: Planck's relation gives the energy of one quantum of radiation.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: The noble gases are placed in which group of the modern periodic table?
questions.explanation: Helium, neon, argon, krypton, xenon and radon form Group 18.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Name the scientist who arranged elements in order of increasing atomic mass and left gaps for undiscovered elements. Why were the gaps important?
questions.answer: Dmitri Mendeleev. He left gaps for elements not yet discovered and predicted their properties; the later discovery of such elements matching his predictions supported his table.
questions.explanation: Predicting eka-aluminium (gallium) and eka-silicon (germanium) made his table widely accepted.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Which of the following is an alkaline earth metal?
questions.explanation: Calcium is in Group 2, the alkaline earth metals.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Across period 3 from sodium to chlorine, the atomic radius:
questions.explanation: The nuclear charge increases while electrons enter the same shell, so the outer electrons are pulled closer.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: An element has the electronic configuration 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁴. It belongs to group:
questions.explanation: It has six valence electrons (3s² 3p⁴), which is Group 16 (this is sulphur).

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Among Na, Mg, Al and Si, which has the highest first ionisation enthalpy?
questions.explanation: Silicon has the highest value of these four (about 786 kJ/mol); Mg is greater than Al only because of its filled 3s subshell, but still lower than Si.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Lithium shows a diagonal relationship with which element?
questions.explanation: Li (Group 1, period 2) resembles Mg (Group 2, period 3) because of similar charge-to-size ratios.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Why are the noble gases chemically unreactive and why do they have high ionisation enthalpies?
questions.answer: They have completely filled outer shells (ns² np⁶, or 1s² for helium), which is a very stable arrangement. Removing an electron from such a shell takes a lot of energy, and they have little tendency to gain or share electrons.
keyPoints: Large energy needed to remove an electron, so high ionisation enthalpy
questions.explanation: The stable octet (duplet for He) explains their inertness.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: The bond between the two hydrogen atoms in an H₂ molecule is:
questions.explanation: The two atoms share a pair of electrons, forming a covalent bond.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: State the octet rule.
questions.answer: Atoms tend to combine, by losing, gaining or sharing electrons, so that each has eight electrons in its outermost shell, like a noble gas.
keyPoints: Atoms gain, lose or share electrons
Aim to have eight electrons in the outer shell
questions.explanation: Hydrogen and helium are exceptions with a duplet.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: In the ammonium ion, NH₄⁺, the fourth N–H bond is formed when:
options: a lone pair of nitrogen is donated to an H⁺ ion
nitrogen transfers an electron to hydrogen
nitrogen gives up all its valence electrons
questions.explanation: The lone pair on NH₃ is shared with H⁺, forming a coordinate (dative) covalent bond.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: The shape of an ammonia (NH₃) molecule is:
questions.explanation: Three bond pairs and one lone pair around nitrogen give a trigonal pyramidal shape.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: How many lone pairs of electrons are there on the oxygen atom in a water molecule?
questions.explanation: Oxygen has six valence electrons; two are used in the O–H bonds, leaving two lone pairs.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Among N₂, O₂, F₂ and H₂, which has the highest bond order?
questions.explanation: N₂ has a bond order of 3, O₂ has 2, and F₂ and H₂ have 1.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: According to molecular orbital theory, which of the following molecules is paramagnetic?
questions.explanation: O₂ has two unpaired electrons in antibonding π* orbitals, so it is paramagnetic; the others have all electrons paired.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: The C=O bonds in carbon dioxide are polar, yet the CO₂ molecule has zero dipole moment. Explain.
questions.answer: CO₂ is linear, so the two equal C=O bond dipoles point in opposite directions and cancel each other. The molecule as a whole is therefore non-polar.
keyPoints: Bond dipoles cancel, net dipole moment is zero
questions.explanation: Molecular polarity depends on both bond polarity and geometry.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: The fluid mosaic model of the plasma membrane was proposed by:
questions.explanation: Singer and Nicolson proposed in 1972 that proteins float in a fluid lipid bilayer.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Name three structures found in plant cells but not in animal cells.
questions.answer: A cell wall, plastids such as chloroplasts, and a large central vacuole.
questions.explanation: Animal cells instead have centrioles, which are generally absent in higher plants.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Which cell organelle contains its own DNA and ribosomes?
questions.explanation: Mitochondria (and chloroplasts) carry their own circular DNA and ribosomes.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: The rough endoplasmic reticulum looks rough because of the presence of:
questions.explanation: Ribosomes attached to the outer surface of the ER give it a rough appearance.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: The cell theory was proposed by:
questions.explanation: Schleiden and Schwann proposed that all plants and animals are made of cells; Virchow added that new cells arise from existing cells.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: A plant cell is placed in a strong salt solution. What will happen?
options: Its protoplast will shrink away from the cell wall
questions.explanation: Water leaves the cell by osmosis, so the protoplast shrinks away from the wall (plasmolysis).

questions.subject: science
questions.q: The inner membrane of a mitochondrion is folded into cristae. The main advantage of this is that it:
options: increases the surface area for respiratory enzymes and ATP synthesis
questions.explanation: Folding gives a larger membrane area on which the electron transport chain and ATP synthase can be arranged.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: A red blood cell bursts when placed in distilled water, but a plant cell in distilled water does not. Why?
questions.answer: Distilled water is hypotonic, so water enters both cells by osmosis. The red blood cell has only a thin plasma membrane and bursts. The plant cell has a rigid cell wall that resists expansion, so it becomes turgid instead.
keyPoints: Water enters by osmosis in a hypotonic medium
Red blood cell has no cell wall, so it bursts
questions.explanation: The cell wall supports the cell against osmotic pressure.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Which sugar is present in DNA?
questions.explanation: DNA stands for deoxyribonucleic acid; its sugar is deoxyribose.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Name the four nitrogenous bases of DNA and state the base-pairing rule.
questions.answer: The bases are adenine, thymine, guanine and cytosine. Adenine pairs with thymine and guanine pairs with cytosine.
questions.explanation: Pairing is through hydrogen bonds between complementary bases.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: The disaccharide sucrose is made up of:
questions.explanation: Table sugar (sucrose) is a glucose unit joined to a fructose unit.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Cholesterol is classified as a:
questions.explanation: Cholesterol is a steroid, which is a type of lipid.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Which of the following is a protein?
questions.explanation: Insulin is a protein hormone; cellulose and glycogen are polysaccharides, and cholesterol is a lipid.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: A competitive inhibitor slows an enzyme-catalysed reaction by:
options: lowering the temperature of the solution
binding to the active site in place of the substrate
questions.explanation: It resembles the substrate in shape, so it competes for the active site; adding more substrate can overcome the inhibition.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Adjacent nucleotides in a single strand of DNA are joined by:
questions.explanation: The phosphate of one nucleotide links to the sugar of the next, forming the sugar-phosphate backbone.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Explain why a DNA molecule with a high proportion of G-C base pairs is more stable (needs more heat to separate its strands) than one with mostly A-T pairs.
questions.answer: A G-C pair is held together by three hydrogen bonds, whereas an A-T pair has only two. More hydrogen bonds mean more energy is needed to separate the strands.
keyPoints: More bonds need more heat to break
questions.explanation: The number of hydrogen bonds between the strands determines the melting temperature.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: In which cell organelle does photosynthesis take place?
questions.explanation: Chloroplasts contain chlorophyll and the enzymes needed for photosynthesis.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Name the raw materials needed for photosynthesis and the two products.
questions.answer: Raw materials: carbon dioxide and water (with light and chlorophyll). Products: glucose (carbohydrate) and oxygen.
questions.explanation: Light energy is converted to chemical energy stored in glucose.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: In the C₃ cycle, the first stable product formed when CO₂ is fixed is a three-carbon compound called:
questions.explanation: RuBisCO adds CO₂ to RuBP, and the product splits into two molecules of 3-phosphoglyceric acid.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: The Krebs cycle takes place in the:
questions.explanation: The enzymes of the Krebs cycle are located in the matrix of the mitochondrion.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: What is the respiratory quotient (RQ) when glucose is completely oxidised in aerobic respiration?
questions.explanation: C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ → 6CO₂ + 6H₂O releases 6 volumes of CO₂ for 6 volumes of O₂, so RQ = 1.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: C₄ plants such as maize show very little photorespiration mainly because:
options: CO₂ is concentrated around RuBisCO in bundle sheath cells
questions.explanation: The C₄ pathway delivers CO₂ to the bundle sheath cells, so RuBisCO works mainly as a carboxylase, not an oxygenase.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Which regions of visible light are most effective for photosynthesis?
questions.explanation: Chlorophylls absorb strongly in the blue and red regions, which gives the highest rate of photosynthesis.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Explain the role of oxygen in aerobic respiration and why it makes the process yield much more ATP than fermentation.
questions.answer: Oxygen is the final acceptor of electrons in the electron transport chain on the inner mitochondrial membrane and combines with hydrogen to form water. This keeps the chain working and the proton gradient driving ATP synthesis, so the glucose is fully oxidised and much more ATP is made.
keyPoints: Oxygen is the final electron acceptor and forms water
Allows the electron transport chain to run and make ATP
Complete oxidation of glucose gives far more ATP than fermentation
questions.explanation: Without oxygen the chain stops and only glycolysis ATP is made.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Which blood cells transport oxygen in the human body?
questions.explanation: Red blood cells (erythrocytes) contain haemoglobin, which carries oxygen.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Which ABO blood group is called the universal donor and which the universal recipient?
questions.answer: Group O is the universal donor (its red cells have no A or B antigens) and group AB is the universal recipient (it has no anti-A or anti-B antibodies).
questions.explanation: This is for red cell transfusion in the ABO system, ignoring other factors such as Rh.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: The volume of air breathed in or out during normal quiet breathing in a healthy adult (tidal volume) is about:
questions.explanation: Tidal volume is about 500 mL per breath, which is roughly 6000 to 8000 mL per minute.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: The natural pacemaker of the human heart is the:
questions.explanation: The SA node, in the wall of the right atrium, generates the impulse that starts each heartbeat.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Which component of blood is mainly involved in clotting?
questions.explanation: Platelets (thrombocytes) release substances that start the clotting cascade.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Which of the following correctly describes inspiration?
options: The diaphragm contracts and flattens, and the pressure in the lungs falls below atmospheric pressure
The diaphragm relaxes and moves upward, and the pressure in the lungs rises
The ribs move downward and inward and the lung volume decreases
The diaphragm contracts and the pressure in the lungs rises above atmospheric pressure
questions.explanation: Contraction of the diaphragm and external intercostal muscles enlarges the thoracic volume, lowering the lung pressure so air flows in.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: In actively respiring tissues, haemoglobin releases more oxygen mainly because there:
options: pCO₂ is low and pH is high
pCO₂ is high and pH is lower
pO₂ is higher than in the lungs
questions.explanation: High pCO₂, lower pH and higher temperature reduce haemoglobin's affinity for oxygen, so it is released where needed.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Why does blockage of a coronary artery cause damage to the heart muscle?
questions.answer: The coronary arteries supply the heart muscle itself with oxygen-rich blood. When one is blocked, the part of the muscle it supplies is starved of oxygen and nutrients and may die, causing a heart attack.
keyPoints: Coronary arteries supply the heart muscle
Blockage cuts off oxygen and nutrients
Affected muscle can be damaged, causing a heart attack
questions.explanation: The heart muscle cannot take its oxygen directly from the blood in its chambers.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Which of the following is the SI unit of temperature?
questions.explanation: The kelvin (K) is the SI base unit of thermodynamic temperature.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: The SI prefix 'kilo' stands for a factor of:
questions.explanation: Kilo means one thousand, 10³.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Which of the following quantities is dimensionless?
questions.explanation: Strain is a ratio of two lengths (change in length / original length), so it has no dimensions.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: One light year (the distance light travels in one year) is approximately:

questions.subject: science
questions.q: The least count of an ordinary metre scale is:
questions.explanation: An ordinary metre scale is marked in millimetres, so its least count is 1 mm.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Write the dimensional formula of the universal gravitational constant G.
questions.answer: From F = G m₁m₂ / r², G = F r² / (m₁m₂) = (MLT⁻²)(L²) / M² = M⁻¹L³T⁻².
keyPoints: Rearrange F = G m₁m₂ / r² for G
Substitute dimensions of F, r and m
questions.explanation: Combining the dimensions of force, length squared and mass squared gives M⁻¹L³T⁻².

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Here v is speed, u is initial speed, a is acceleration, x is distance and t is time. Which equation is dimensionally correct?
questions.explanation: In v² = u² + 2ax every term has dimensions L²T⁻². In the other equations the dimensions of the two sides do not match.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Assume the time period T of a simple pendulum depends only on its mass m, length l and the acceleration due to gravity g. Use dimensional analysis to find how T depends on these quantities.
questions.answer: Let T = k m^a l^b g^c. Comparing dimensions: M: a = 0; L: b + c = 0; T: −2c = 1, so c = −½ and b = ½. Hence T ∝ √(l/g), independent of the mass.
keyPoints: Write T = k m^a l^b g^c
Equate powers of M, L, T: a = 0, b = ½, c = −½
T is proportional to √(l/g) and does not depend on m
questions.explanation: The constant k (equal to 2π) cannot be found by dimensional analysis.

questions.subject: science
questions.topic: Motion in a Straight Line and in a Plane
questions.q: The rate of change of velocity of a body is called:
questions.explanation: Acceleration is defined as change in velocity per unit time.

questions.subject: science
questions.topic: Motion in a Straight Line and in a Plane
questions.q: What is the acceleration of a body moving with a uniform (constant) velocity?
questions.explanation: Velocity is not changing, so the acceleration is zero.

questions.subject: science
questions.topic: Motion in a Straight Line and in a Plane
questions.q: In uniform circular motion, the direction of the velocity of the body at any point is along the:
questions.explanation: The velocity is always tangential to the path.

questions.subject: science
questions.topic: Motion in a Straight Line and in a Plane
questions.q: A ball is thrown vertically upward with a speed of 30 m/s. Taking g = 10 m/s², how long does it take to reach its highest point?
questions.explanation: At the top v = 0, so t = u/g = 30/10 = 3 s.

questions.subject: science
questions.topic: Motion in a Straight Line and in a Plane
questions.q: A 100 m long train moves at a constant speed of 20 m/s. How long does it take to pass a signal pole completely?
questions.explanation: The train must travel its own length: t = 100 / 20 = 5 s.

questions.subject: science
questions.topic: Motion in a Straight Line and in a Plane
questions.q: A car increases its speed uniformly from 10 m/s to 30 m/s in 5 s. Find its acceleration and the distance covered in this time.
questions.answer: a = (30 − 10)/5 = 4 m/s². Distance = (average speed) × time = ((10 + 30)/2) × 5 = 100 m.
keyPoints: Acceleration = change in velocity / time = 4 m/s²
questions.explanation: For uniform acceleration the average velocity is the mean of the initial and final velocities.

questions.subject: science
questions.topic: Motion in a Straight Line and in a Plane
questions.q: A particle moves in a circle of radius 2 m at a constant speed of 4 m/s. What is the magnitude of its acceleration?
questions.explanation: Centripetal acceleration = v²/r = 16/2 = 8 m/s², directed towards the centre.

questions.subject: science
questions.topic: Motion in a Straight Line and in a Plane
questions.q: A car moves around a circular track at a constant speed. Is the car accelerating? Explain.
questions.answer: Yes. Acceleration is the rate of change of velocity, a vector. The speed is constant, but the direction of the velocity changes continuously, so the velocity changes and the car has an acceleration directed towards the centre of the track.
keyPoints: Acceleration is the change of velocity, including its direction
questions.explanation: Constant speed does not mean constant velocity.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: The inertia of a body depends on its:
questions.explanation: Inertia is a measure of the resistance to change in motion and is measured by mass.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Which of the following is the SI unit of impulse?
questions.explanation: Impulse = force × time, so its unit is N s (equal to kg m/s).

questions.subject: science
questions.q: The force of friction between two surfaces in contact always acts:
options: opposite to the relative motion, or the tendency of relative motion, between them
in the direction of the relative motion
towards the centre of the Earth
questions.explanation: Friction opposes sliding or the tendency to slide between the surfaces.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: A 1000 kg car moving at 20 m/s is brought to rest uniformly in 10 s. What is the average braking force?

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Taking g = 9.8 m/s², what is the weight of a 50 kg person on the Earth?
questions.explanation: Weight = mg = 50 × 9.8 = 490 N.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: State the law of conservation of linear momentum and give one example.
questions.answer: If no external force acts on a system, the total linear momentum of the system remains constant. Example: the recoil of a gun when a bullet is fired, or the collision of two bodies.
keyPoints: Total momentum is constant when the net external force is zero
Example such as gun recoil or a collision
questions.explanation: It follows from Newton's second and third laws.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: A 5 kg block slides down a smooth (frictionless) incline making an angle of 30° with the horizontal. Taking g = 10 m/s², its acceleration is:
questions.explanation: The component of gravity along the incline gives a = g sin 30° = 10 × 0.5 = 5 m/s²; the mass does not matter.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: A 10 kg block lies on a rough horizontal floor (coefficient of kinetic friction 0.3). A horizontal force of 50 N pulls it. Taking g = 10 m/s², find the acceleration of the block.
questions.answer: Normal force = mg = 100 N, so kinetic friction = 0.3 × 100 = 30 N. Net force = 50 − 30 = 20 N. Acceleration = 20/10 = 2 m/s².
questions.explanation: Newton's second law is applied to the net force along the floor.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: A constant force F moves a body through a distance s in the direction of the force. The work done is:
questions.explanation: When force and displacement are in the same direction, W = Fs.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: The energy stored in a stretched spring is:
questions.explanation: A deformed spring stores elastic potential energy, ½kx².

questions.subject: science
questions.q: One horsepower is approximately equal to:
questions.explanation: 1 horsepower is about 746 watts.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: What is the kinetic energy of a 4 kg body moving at 5 m/s?

questions.subject: science
questions.q: A force of 10 N acts on a body at 60° to the direction of its displacement, and the body moves 4 m. The work done by the force is:

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Distinguish between a conservative force and a non-conservative force, giving one example of each.
questions.answer: The work done by a conservative force depends only on the starting and end points, not on the path, and is zero over a closed path; gravity is an example. For a non-conservative force the work depends on the path taken; friction is an example.
keyPoints: Conservative: work independent of path, zero for a closed loop
Non-conservative: work depends on the path
questions.explanation: Potential energy can be defined only for conservative forces.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: A ball dropped from a height h bounces back up to a height h/2. What fraction of its mechanical energy is lost in the bounce?
questions.explanation: Its energy before and after the bounce is mgh and mgh/2, so half of it is lost.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: A person carries a 20 kg suitcase horizontally for 10 m at constant speed. Does the person do work against gravity? Explain.
questions.answer: No work is done against gravity. The force needed to support the suitcase is vertical, but the displacement is horizontal, so the angle between them is 90° and W = Fs cos 90° = 0.
keyPoints: Supporting force is vertical, displacement horizontal
So the work done against gravity is zero
questions.explanation: The person does work in the body (physiological effort), but not in the physics sense on the suitcase.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: The value of the universal gravitational constant G is:
questions.explanation: G is about 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻².

questions.subject: science
questions.q: The gravitational force between two masses is always:
options: repulsive at short and attractive at long distances
questions.explanation: Gravity between two masses is always an attractive force.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: The escape velocity of a body from the Earth does NOT depend on the:
questions.explanation: v = √(2GM/R), which has no term for the mass of the escaping body.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: The acceleration due to gravity on the surface of the Moon is approximately:
questions.explanation: The Moon's g is about one-sixth of the Earth's, roughly 1.6 m/s².

questions.subject: science
questions.q: The time period of a satellite orbiting very close to the Earth's surface is about:

questions.subject: science
questions.q: State Newton's law of gravitation and write its mathematical form.
questions.answer: Every body attracts every other body with a force directly proportional to the product of their masses and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between them: F = G m₁m₂ / r².
keyPoints: Proportional to the product of the masses
Inversely proportional to the square of the distance
questions.explanation: The force acts along the line joining the centres of the two bodies.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: A planet has 4 times the mass of the Earth and 2 times the radius of the Earth. The acceleration due to gravity at its surface is:
questions.explanation: g' = GM'/R'² = G(4M)/(2R)² = GM/R² = g.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Two people of mass 60 kg each stand 1 m apart. Estimate the gravitational force between them (G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻²) and explain why they do not feel it.
questions.answer: F = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ × 60 × 60 / 1² ≈ 2.4 × 10⁻⁷ N. This is extremely small compared to forces such as their own weight or friction, because G is so small and their masses are small. It only becomes noticeable when one of the masses is as large as a planet.
keyPoints: G is very small and the masses are small
Much smaller than the weight or friction acting on them
questions.explanation: Gravity is noticeable only for very massive bodies.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Which of the following is a mixture?
questions.explanation: Air is a mixture of nitrogen, oxygen and other gases; the others are pure substances.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: One atomic mass unit (u) is defined as exactly 1/12 of the mass of:
questions.explanation: The unified atomic mass unit is defined using the carbon-12 atom.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: What is the molar mass of sodium chloride, NaCl? (Na = 23, Cl = 35.5)

questions.subject: science
questions.q: How many moles are present in 5.85 g of sodium chloride? (Molar mass = 58.5 g/mol)

questions.subject: science
questions.q: What is the molarity of a solution containing 0.5 mol of solute in 250 mL of solution?
questions.explanation: Molarity = 0.5 mol / 0.25 L = 2 M.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: State the law of multiple proportions and illustrate it with carbon monoxide and carbon dioxide.
questions.answer: When two elements form more than one compound, the different masses of one element that combine with a fixed mass of the other are in a simple whole-number ratio. In CO, 12 g of carbon combines with 16 g of oxygen; in CO₂, 12 g of carbon combines with 32 g of oxygen. The ratio of oxygen masses is 1 : 2.
keyPoints: Masses of one element combining with a fixed mass of the other are in simple whole-number ratio
CO: 16 g O per 12 g C; CO₂: 32 g O per 12 g C
questions.explanation: The law was proposed by Dalton.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Which of the following contains the greatest number of molecules? (H = 1, C = 12, O = 16)
questions.explanation: Moles are 1/2 (H₂), 1/16 (CH₄), 1/32 (O₂) and 1/44 (CO₂); the lightest molecule gives the most moles in 1 g.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: 100 mL of 2 M HCl is diluted with water to a total volume of 500 mL. What is the molarity of the diluted solution?
questions.answer: The moles of HCl stay the same: M₁V₁ = M₂V₂, so 2 × 100 = M₂ × 500 and M₂ = 0.4 M.
keyPoints: Moles of solute do not change on dilution
questions.explanation: Moles of HCl = 2 × 0.1 = 0.2 mol, and 0.2 / 0.5 L = 0.4 M.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Which subatomic particle carries a negative charge?
questions.explanation: Electrons carry a negative charge; protons and alpha particles are positive and neutrons are neutral.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Which scientist proposed an atomic model with electrons moving in fixed, quantised orbits?
questions.explanation: Niels Bohr proposed that electrons move only in certain allowed orbits without radiating energy.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: How many protons are present in an atom of carbon-14? (Atomic number of carbon = 6)
questions.explanation: The number of protons equals the atomic number, 6.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: How many orbitals are there in a p subshell?
questions.explanation: For l = 1 there are 2l + 1 = 3 orbitals (px, py, pz).

questions.subject: science
questions.q: What is the shape of an s orbital?
questions.explanation: An s orbital is spherically symmetrical about the nucleus.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: State Heisenberg's uncertainty principle.
questions.answer: It is impossible to determine both the exact position and the exact momentum (or velocity) of a microscopic particle such as an electron at the same time. The product of the uncertainties is at least h/4π.
keyPoints: Position and momentum cannot both be known exactly
Δx · Δp is at least h/4π
Important for very small particles like electrons
questions.explanation: It rules out well-defined orbits for electrons.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: The energy of the electron in the nth orbit of a hydrogen atom is −13.6/n² eV. What is the energy in the first excited state (n = 2)?

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Find the number of protons, neutrons and electrons in the chloride ion ³⁵Cl⁻ (atomic number 17).
questions.answer: Protons = 17. Neutrons = 35 − 17 = 18. Electrons = 17 + 1 = 18, since the ion carries one extra electron.
keyPoints: Electrons = 18 because of the negative charge
questions.explanation: A negative ion has more electrons than protons.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: The elements of Group 1 (except hydrogen) are known as:
questions.explanation: Li, Na, K, Rb, Cs and Fr form the alkali metals.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Which of the following is a metalloid?
questions.explanation: Silicon has properties between those of metals and non-metals.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: The element with atomic number 20 (calcium) belongs to which group?
questions.explanation: Its configuration ends in 4s², so it is in Group 2.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Among the alkali metals Li, Na, K and Cs, the most reactive is:
questions.explanation: Reactivity of alkali metals increases down the group because the outer electron is lost more easily.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Which halogen has the most negative electron gain enthalpy?
questions.explanation: Fluorine's small size causes electron repulsion in its compact 2p subshell, so chlorine releases the most energy.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Define electronegativity. How does it change down a group?
questions.answer: Electronegativity is the tendency of an atom in a molecule to attract the shared pair of electrons towards itself. It decreases down a group because the atoms become larger and the bonding electrons are farther from the nucleus.
keyPoints: Tendency of an atom to attract shared electrons in a bond
questions.explanation: It is a relative scale (for example, Pauling's).

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Which of the following oxides is amphoteric?
questions.explanation: Al₂O₃ reacts with both acids and bases; Na₂O and MgO are basic and CO₂ is acidic.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Why is a cation smaller than its parent atom, while an anion is larger than its parent atom?
questions.answer: A cation has lost electrons, often a whole outer shell, and the same nuclear charge now pulls fewer electrons, so the radius shrinks. An anion has gained electrons, which increases electron-electron repulsion while the nuclear charge is unchanged, so it expands.
keyPoints: Cation: fewer electrons, same nuclear charge, pulled in more strongly
Nuclear charge is unchanged in both cases
questions.explanation: Compare Na (radius larger) with Na⁺ and Cl with Cl⁻.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: How many valence electrons does a carbon atom have?
questions.explanation: Carbon has the configuration 1s² 2s² 2p², so four valence electrons.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Which of the following compounds has ionic bonding?
questions.explanation: MgO consists of Mg²⁺ and O²⁻ ions; the others are covalent compounds.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Which of these molecules contains a double bond between its two atoms?
questions.explanation: In O₂, each oxygen atom shares two electron pairs with the other, forming a double bond.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: In boron trifluoride (BF₃), the boron atom is hybridised as:
questions.explanation: Boron forms three sigma bonds with no lone pair, so it is sp² hybridised and the molecule is trigonal planar.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: The shape of the sulphur hexafluoride (SF₆) molecule is:
questions.explanation: Six bond pairs and no lone pairs around sulphur give an octahedral shape.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Define bond length and bond enthalpy.
