questions.answer: Bond length is the equilibrium distance between the nuclei of two bonded atoms. Bond enthalpy is the amount of energy required to break one mole of a particular bond in gaseous molecules.
keyPoints: Bond length: distance between nuclei of bonded atoms
Bond enthalpy: energy to break one mole of bonds
Higher bond order gives shorter bond and higher enthalpy
questions.explanation: A shorter bond is generally stronger.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Among HF, HCl, HBr and HI, which has the highest boiling point?
questions.explanation: HF molecules form strong hydrogen bonds; the others rise in boiling point only gradually with size.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: The dipole moment of NH₃ is larger than that of NF₃, although fluorine is more electronegative than hydrogen. Explain.
questions.answer: In NH₃ the N-H bond dipoles point towards nitrogen and the lone pair dipole also points the same way, so they add up. In NF₃ the N-F bond dipoles point towards fluorine, opposite to the lone pair dipole, so they partly cancel and the net dipole moment is small.
keyPoints: NH₃: bond dipoles and lone-pair dipole in the same direction
NF₃: bond dipoles oppose the lone-pair dipole
Partial cancellation gives a smaller net dipole in NF₃
questions.explanation: Direction of dipoles, not just their size, decides the net dipole moment.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Which cell organelle is sometimes called the 'suicide bag' of the cell?
questions.explanation: If a lysosome bursts, its digestive enzymes can destroy the cell.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: The plasma membrane is made mainly of:
questions.explanation: The membrane is a lipid bilayer (mostly phospholipids) with embedded proteins.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Which organelle modifies, sorts and packages proteins for secretion?
questions.explanation: The Golgi apparatus processes proteins and lipids from the ER and packs them into vesicles.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: The nucleolus in the nucleus is the main site of synthesis of:
questions.explanation: rRNA is made in the nucleolus and combined with proteins to form ribosome subunits.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: In animal cells, centrioles help in:
options: forming spindle fibres during cell division
questions.explanation: Centrioles organise the spindle fibres used to separate chromosomes.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: List three functions of the nucleus in a cell.
questions.answer: The nucleus contains the genetic material (DNA in chromosomes), controls the activities of the cell by directing protein synthesis, and takes part in cell division and heredity. The nucleolus makes ribosomal RNA.
keyPoints: Controls cell activities through gene expression
Involved in cell division and heredity
questions.explanation: The nucleus is the control centre of the eukaryotic cell.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: A gland cell that secretes large amounts of digestive enzymes (proteins) would be expected to have well-developed:
questions.explanation: Proteins are made on the rough ER and packaged and secreted through the Golgi apparatus.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: How does facilitated diffusion differ from active transport across the plasma membrane?
questions.answer: Facilitated diffusion moves substances down their concentration gradient through carrier or channel proteins without using energy. Active transport moves substances against the gradient and needs energy from ATP.
keyPoints: Facilitated diffusion: down the gradient, no ATP
Active transport: against the gradient, uses ATP
questions.explanation: Direction of movement and the energy requirement are the key differences.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Glucose is an example of a:
questions.explanation: Glucose is a single sugar unit, a monosaccharide.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Which element is present in all proteins but not in simple carbohydrates or fats?
questions.explanation: The amino group of every amino acid contains nitrogen.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: In animals, carbohydrate is stored in the liver and muscles as:
questions.explanation: Glycogen is the storage polysaccharide of animals.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: The double helix model of DNA was proposed by:
questions.explanation: James Watson and Francis Crick proposed the double helix structure of DNA in 1953.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Enzymes speed up chemical reactions by:
options: being used up in the reaction
questions.explanation: Enzymes provide an alternative pathway with a lower activation energy, and they are not used up.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Distinguish between the primary and secondary structures of a protein.
questions.answer: The primary structure is the linear sequence of amino acids in the polypeptide chain. The secondary structure is the regular folding of the chain, such as the alpha helix and beta pleated sheet, held by hydrogen bonds.
keyPoints: Secondary: alpha helix or beta sheet
Secondary structure is held by hydrogen bonds
questions.explanation: The tertiary and quaternary structures build further on these two levels.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: When egg white is boiled it coagulates. Which level of protein structure is NOT destroyed by this heating?
questions.explanation: Heat breaks the weak bonds that maintain the folded shape, but the strong peptide bonds, and so the amino acid sequence, remain.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Humans digest starch but cannot digest cellulose, though both are polymers of glucose. Explain why.
questions.answer: In starch the glucose units are joined by alpha-glycosidic linkages, which our digestive enzyme (amylase) can break. In cellulose they are joined by beta-glycosidic linkages, and humans lack the enzyme cellulase to break them.
keyPoints: Starch has alpha linkages, cellulose has beta linkages
questions.explanation: The type of linkage, not the monomer, decides digestibility.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Plants take in carbon dioxide from the air mainly through tiny pores called:
questions.explanation: Stomata, mostly on the leaf surface, control the exchange of CO₂ and O₂.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Glycolysis converts one molecule of glucose into two molecules of:
questions.explanation: Glucose (6 carbons) is broken down into two three-carbon pyruvic acid molecules.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: How many carbon atoms are present in a molecule of pyruvic acid?
questions.explanation: Pyruvic acid is CH₃COCOOH, a three-carbon compound.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Which of the following is a C₄ plant?
questions.explanation: Maize, sugarcane and sorghum are C₄ plants; wheat, rice and potato are C₃ plants.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: The energy in an ATP molecule is stored mainly in:
questions.explanation: Breaking the terminal phosphate bond releases energy that cells use for work.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Give three differences between photosynthesis and respiration.
questions.answer: Photosynthesis takes place only in cells with chlorophyll in light, stores energy in glucose, uses CO₂ and water and releases oxygen. Respiration takes place in all living cells, day and night, releases energy from glucose, uses oxygen and gives CO₂ and water.
keyPoints: Photosynthesis stores energy; respiration releases it
Photosynthesis uses CO₂ and releases O₂; respiration does the opposite
Respiration occurs in all living cells; photosynthesis only in green cells
questions.explanation: The two processes are complementary in the energy cycle of living things.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: The rate of photosynthesis of a leaf does not increase any further when the light intensity is raised. The most likely reason is that:
options: the leaf has stopped absorbing light completely
another factor such as the CO₂ concentration or temperature has become limiting
questions.explanation: When one factor is in short supply it limits the rate, and increasing another factor produces no further rise.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: A plant respires all day, yet it releases oxygen during the day. Explain.
questions.answer: During the day the rate of photosynthesis is higher than the rate of respiration, so the oxygen produced in photosynthesis is more than the oxygen used in respiration, and the excess is released. At the compensation point the two are equal and there is no net gas exchange.
keyPoints: Both processes occur in the day
questions.explanation: At night only respiration occurs, so there is a net uptake of oxygen.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: The trachea is prevented from collapsing by rings of:
questions.explanation: C-shaped cartilage rings keep the windpipe open.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Exchange of gases between air and blood in the lungs takes place in the:
questions.explanation: Alveoli have thin walls and a rich blood supply, which suits gas exchange.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Which blood vessel carries deoxygenated blood from the heart to the lungs?
questions.explanation: The pulmonary artery carries deoxygenated blood from the right ventricle to the lungs.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: In a healthy adult at rest the cardiac cycle lasts about:
questions.explanation: At about 72 beats per minute, each cardiac cycle takes roughly 0.8 seconds.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: The first heart sound ('lub') is produced by the closure of the:
questions.explanation: The first sound occurs when the atrioventricular valves close at the start of ventricular contraction.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: State three differences between arteries and veins.
questions.answer: Arteries carry blood away from the heart, have thick elastic walls and carry blood under high pressure (mostly oxygenated, except the pulmonary artery). Veins carry blood to the heart, have thinner walls, carry blood under low pressure and have valves.
keyPoints: Arteries away from heart, veins to heart
Arteries have thick walls, veins thinner walls
Veins have valves; arteries do not
questions.explanation: The structural differences are related to the pressure of blood in each vessel.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: A patient with emphysema has breathing difficulty mainly because:
options: there are too many red blood cells
the heart valves do not close
the alveolar walls are damaged, which reduces the surface area for gas exchange
questions.explanation: In emphysema the alveolar walls break down, so less surface area is available for exchange of oxygen and carbon dioxide.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Why does a person suffering from anaemia feel breathless on mild exertion?
questions.answer: Anaemia means low haemoglobin or too few red cells, so the blood carries less oxygen. During exertion the tissues need more oxygen, so the person must breathe faster and the heart beats faster to compensate, which feels like breathlessness.
keyPoints: Low haemoglobin means reduced oxygen-carrying capacity
Tissues need more oxygen on exertion
Breathing and heart rate rise to compensate
questions.explanation: Oxygen delivery depends on haemoglobin and blood flow.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Which of the following is a base (fundamental) quantity in the SI system?
questions.explanation: Electric current is one of the seven base quantities; force, energy and pressure are derived.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: What are significant figures? State how many significant figures there are in 0.0070.
questions.answer: Significant figures are the reliably known digits in a measured value, plus the first uncertain digit. 0.0070 has two significant figures (7 and the final 0), because leading zeros are not significant.
keyPoints: Digits that carry meaning about the precision of a measurement
questions.explanation: A trailing zero after the decimal point shows the measurement was precise to that digit.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: What is the dimensional formula of linear momentum?
questions.explanation: Momentum = mass × velocity = M × LT⁻¹ = MLT⁻¹.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: A length of 0.00025 m expressed in millimetres is:

questions.subject: science
questions.q: How many significant figures are there in the measurement 100.0 g?
questions.explanation: The zeros after the 1 are significant here because the decimal point is shown, so all four digits count.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: The side of a cube is measured as 2.0 cm with an uncertainty of 0.1 cm. What is the percentage uncertainty in its volume?
questions.explanation: The error in the side is 5%, and volume depends on the cube of the side, so the error in volume is 3 × 5% = 15%.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: The product of force and time has the same dimensions as:
questions.explanation: Force × time = MLT⁻² × T = MLT⁻¹, which is the dimension of momentum (impulse equals change in momentum).

questions.subject: science
questions.q: A quantity is calculated as P = a³b² / (c√d). The percentage errors in a, b, c and d are 1%, 2%, 3% and 4% respectively. Find the maximum percentage error in P.
keyPoints: Multiply each percentage error by the power of that quantity
Add the errors for the maximum error
questions.explanation: In products and quotients the percentage errors add up, each weighted by the power.

questions.subject: science
questions.topic: Motion in a Straight Line and in a Plane
questions.q: Speed is:
options: always zero for a moving body
questions.explanation: Speed has magnitude only, so it is a scalar.

questions.subject: science
questions.topic: Motion in a Straight Line and in a Plane
questions.q: What does the area under a velocity-time graph represent?
questions.answer: The area under a velocity-time graph gives the displacement of the body in that time interval.
keyPoints: Area under v-t graph is the displacement
For motion in one direction it equals the distance
questions.explanation: Displacement is the sum of velocity × small time intervals.

questions.subject: science
questions.topic: Motion in a Straight Line and in a Plane
questions.q: A bus slows from 20 m/s to 10 m/s in 5 s with uniform retardation. Its acceleration is:
questions.explanation: a = (10 − 20)/5 = −2 m/s²; the negative sign shows it is slowing down.

questions.subject: science
questions.topic: Motion in a Straight Line and in a Plane
questions.q: A stone is thrown vertically upward with a speed of 20 m/s. Taking g = 10 m/s² and ignoring air resistance, how long does it take to return to the thrower's hand?
questions.explanation: Time to rise is u/g = 2 s, and the descent takes equally long, so the total is 4 s.

questions.subject: science
questions.topic: Motion in a Straight Line and in a Plane
questions.q: The position of a particle moving along a straight line is x = 3t² (x in metres, t in seconds). What is its velocity at t = 2 s?
questions.explanation: v = dx/dt = 6t, so at t = 2 s the velocity is 12 m/s.

questions.subject: science
questions.topic: Motion in a Straight Line and in a Plane
questions.q: A body dropped from a height h takes time t to reach the ground. How long would it take to fall from a height 4h?
questions.explanation: Since h = ½gt², t is proportional to √h; quadrupling h doubles the time.

questions.subject: science
questions.topic: Motion in a Straight Line and in a Plane
questions.q: A boat can move at 5 m/s in still water. It is steered straight across a 100 m wide river flowing at 3 m/s. How far downstream is it when it reaches the opposite bank?
questions.explanation: The crossing takes 100/5 = 20 s, during which the river carries it 3 × 20 = 60 m downstream.

questions.subject: science
questions.topic: Motion in a Straight Line and in a Plane
questions.q: Using the formula for range, explain why a projectile launched with a fixed speed has its maximum horizontal range when the angle of projection is 45°.
questions.answer: The range is R = u² sin 2θ / g. For a given speed, R is largest when sin 2θ has its maximum value of 1, i.e. 2θ = 90°, so θ = 45°.
questions.explanation: The maximum range is u²/g.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: A force of 1 N acts on a body of mass 1 kg. The acceleration produced is:

questions.subject: science
questions.q: What is friction? State two ways of reducing it.
questions.answer: Friction is the force that opposes the relative motion, or the tendency of motion, between two surfaces in contact. It can be reduced by lubrication (oil or grease) and by using ball bearings or wheels, or by polishing the surfaces.
keyPoints: Opposes relative motion between surfaces in contact
Reduce it by ball bearings or wheels
questions.explanation: Rolling friction is smaller than sliding friction.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: A rocket moves upward by throwing out hot gases downward. This is best explained by:
options: Newton's third law and conservation of momentum
questions.explanation: The rocket pushes the gases backward and, by the third law and momentum conservation, the gases push the rocket forward.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Limiting friction is:
options: the friction acting on a body that is already sliding
the maximum value of static friction
the friction acting on a rolling body
the friction when no force is applied
questions.explanation: Static friction increases with the applied force up to a maximum, called limiting friction, beyond which sliding begins.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: A body of mass 2 kg, initially at rest, is acted on by a constant force of 10 N for 3 s. What is its final speed?

questions.subject: science
questions.q: A 70 kg man stands on a weighing scale in a lift that is accelerating downward at 3 m/s². Taking g = 10 m/s², the reading of the scale is:
questions.explanation: N = m(g − a) = 70 × 7 = 490 N, less than his actual weight.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: A car travels round a level circular road of radius 40 m. The coefficient of friction between the tyres and road is 0.4 and g = 10 m/s². The maximum speed at which it can take the turn without skidding is about:
questions.explanation: Friction supplies the centripetal force, so μmg = mv²/r and v = √(μrg) = √160 ≈ 12.6 m/s.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: A 0.1 kg ball hits a wall at 10 m/s and rebounds at 10 m/s in the opposite direction. The contact lasts 0.01 s. Find the change in momentum and the average force on the ball.
questions.answer: Taking the initial direction as positive, the change in momentum = (−0.1 × 10) − (0.1 × 10) = −2 kg m/s, so its magnitude is 2 kg m/s. The average force = 2 / 0.01 = 200 N, directed away from the wall.
keyPoints: Reversal of velocity: Δp = 2mv = 2 kg m/s
questions.explanation: A short contact time gives a large average force.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: 'Energy can neither be created nor destroyed but only changed from one form to another.' This statement is called the law of:
questions.explanation: This is the statement of conservation of energy.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Define power and state its SI unit.
questions.answer: Power is the rate of doing work, or the work done per unit time. Its SI unit is the watt (1 W = 1 J/s).
questions.explanation: Power can also be written as force × velocity.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: A body of mass 2 kg, initially at rest, is pushed by a constant force of 4 N through a distance of 5 m on a smooth surface. Its kinetic energy at the end is:
questions.explanation: By the work-energy theorem, KE = work done = 4 × 5 = 20 J.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: A machine does 3000 J of work in 20 s. Its power is:

questions.subject: science
questions.q: A 1 kg ball falls freely from a height of 5 m. Taking g = 10 m/s² and ignoring air resistance, its kinetic energy just before it hits the ground is:
questions.explanation: All the potential energy mgh = 1 × 10 × 5 = 50 J is converted into kinetic energy.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: A car engine works at constant power. If the speed of the car is doubled, the driving force provided by the engine becomes:
questions.explanation: P = Fv, so for constant P the force is inversely proportional to the speed.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: A pendulum bob on a 0.8 m string is released from a point where the string is horizontal. Taking g = 10 m/s² and ignoring air resistance, its speed at the lowest point is:
questions.explanation: The bob falls through 0.8 m, so ½mv² = mgh gives v = √(2 × 10 × 0.8) = 4 m/s.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: A student of mass 50 kg climbs a staircase 3 m high in 10 s. Taking g = 10 m/s², find the average power she develops.
questions.explanation: This is the useful power in raising her body weight.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: The force that keeps the Earth moving in its orbit around the Sun is:
questions.explanation: The Sun's gravitational attraction provides the centripetal force for planetary orbits.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: What is meant by free fall?
questions.answer: Free fall is the motion of a body under the influence of gravity alone, with no other force such as air resistance acting on it. All bodies then fall with the same acceleration g.
keyPoints: Same acceleration g for all bodies
questions.explanation: A freely falling body is weightless in the sense that there is no normal reaction on it.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: The weight of a body at the centre of the Earth is:
options: twice its weight on the surface
questions.explanation: At the centre the gravitational pulls from all sides cancel, so g and weight become zero.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: The mass of the Earth is approximately:
questions.explanation: The Earth's mass is about 6 × 10²⁴ kg.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: At which point in its orbit is a planet's speed the greatest?
options: At the point farthest from the Sun
At the point nearest to the Sun
Midway between the nearest and farthest points
Its speed is the same everywhere
questions.explanation: By the law of areas, the planet moves fastest when it is closest to the Sun.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: A satellite moves in a circular orbit around the Earth. If the radius of the orbit is made 4 times larger, its orbital speed will:
questions.explanation: Orbital speed v = √(GM/r), so quadrupling r halves v.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Taking the gravitational potential energy at infinite distance as zero, the potential energy of a mass m on the surface of the Earth (mass M, radius R) is:
questions.explanation: Gravity is attractive, so work must be done to take the mass to infinity; the potential energy is negative, −GMm/R.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: The Moon has almost no atmosphere. Explain this using the idea of escape velocity.
questions.answer: The Moon's escape velocity (about 2.4 km/s) is small because of its small mass and radius. Gas molecules can reach speeds comparable to this, so gases escape from the Moon over time, whereas the Earth's much larger escape velocity (11.2 km/s) holds on to its atmosphere.
keyPoints: Moon's escape velocity is low (about 2.4 km/s)
Gas molecules can reach such speeds and escape
Earth's higher escape velocity retains its atmosphere
questions.explanation: Escape velocity depends on √(GM/R).

questions.subject: science
questions.q: The SI unit of the amount of a substance is the:
questions.explanation: The mole (mol) is the SI base unit for amount of substance.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: What is meant by one mole of a substance? How is it related to Avogadro's number?
questions.answer: One mole is the amount of a substance that contains as many particles (atoms, molecules or ions) as there are atoms in 12 g of carbon-12. This number is Avogadro's number, 6.022 × 10²³.
keyPoints: Equal to the number of atoms in 12 g of carbon-12
Mass of one mole is the molar mass
questions.explanation: The mole links the atomic scale to laboratory quantities.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: How many moles are present in 22 g of carbon dioxide? (C = 12, O = 16)
questions.explanation: Molar mass of CO₂ = 44 g/mol; 22 / 44 = 0.5 mol.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Which law states that equal volumes of all gases under the same conditions of temperature and pressure contain equal numbers of molecules?
questions.explanation: This is Avogadro's law.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: The empirical formula of glucose, C₆H₁₂O₆, is:
questions.explanation: The simplest whole-number ratio of C : H : O in glucose is 1 : 2 : 1.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: What mass of NaOH is needed to prepare 250 mL of a 0.1 M solution? (Na = 23, O = 16, H = 1)

questions.subject: science
questions.q: In the reaction N₂ + 3H₂ → 2NH₃, what mass of ammonia is formed from 28 g of nitrogen if hydrogen is in excess? (N = 14, H = 1)
questions.explanation: 28 g of N₂ is 1 mol, which gives 2 mol of NH₃ = 2 × 17 = 34 g.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: 3 g of carbon is burnt in 4 g of oxygen: C + O₂ → CO₂. Identify the limiting reagent and find the mass of CO₂ formed. (C = 12, O = 16)
questions.answer: Moles of C = 3/12 = 0.25 mol; moles of O₂ = 4/32 = 0.125 mol. Since 1 mol of C needs 1 mol of O₂, oxygen is the limiting reagent. CO₂ formed = 0.125 mol × 44 = 5.5 g.
questions.explanation: The limiting reagent decides how much product can form.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: A neutral atom of an element with atomic number 11 has how many electrons?
questions.explanation: A neutral atom has as many electrons as protons, 11.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Distinguish between an orbit and an orbital.
questions.answer: An orbit (Bohr model) is a fixed circular path in which an electron revolves around the nucleus. An orbital is a three-dimensional region around the nucleus where the probability of finding an electron is high, and it can hold a maximum of two electrons.
keyPoints: Orbit: definite path in the Bohr model
Orbital: region of high probability of finding the electron
An orbital holds at most two electrons
questions.explanation: The orbital concept follows from the quantum mechanical model.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Which quantum number determines the shape of an orbital?
questions.explanation: l = 0, 1, 2, 3 correspond to s, p, d, f orbitals of different shapes.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: What is the maximum number of electrons that can be accommodated in a d subshell?
questions.explanation: A d subshell has 5 orbitals, each holding 2 electrons, so 10 electrons.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: The electronic configuration [Ar] 3d¹⁰ 4s¹ belongs to the element:
questions.explanation: Copper has the configuration [Ar] 3d¹⁰ 4s¹ because a filled d subshell is extra stable.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Which of the following pairs of ions has the same number of electrons?
questions.explanation: K⁺ and Cl⁻ each have 18 electrons; in the other pairs the numbers differ (10 and 18, 10 and 18, 2 and 10).

questions.subject: science
questions.q: An electron and a proton move with the same speed. Which has the shorter de Broglie wavelength?
questions.explanation: λ = h/mv; the proton has the larger mass, so its wavelength is smaller.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Calculate the de Broglie wavelength of a 0.1 kg ball moving at 10 m/s (h = 6.626 × 10⁻³⁴ J s). Why do we not observe this wavelength?
questions.answer: λ = h/mv = 6.626 × 10⁻³⁴ / (0.1 × 10) = 6.626 × 10⁻³⁴ m. This is far too small to be detected, so wave behaviour is not observed for large objects.
keyPoints: Too small to detect for a macroscopic body
questions.explanation: Wave nature matters only for particles of very small mass.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Elements in the same group of the periodic table have the same:
questions.explanation: Elements in a group have similar outer electron configurations, which gives them similar properties.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: How many elements are present in the second and in the third periods of the modern periodic table?
questions.answer: Each of the second and third periods has 8 elements (lithium to neon, and sodium to argon).
keyPoints: Second period: Li to Ne, 8 elements
Third period: Na to Ar, 8 elements
questions.explanation: These are called short periods.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Lanthanoids and actinoids belong to which block of the periodic table?
questions.explanation: In these elements the last electron enters the 4f or 5f subshell.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Which of the following is a d-block (transition) element?
questions.explanation: Iron has the configuration [Ar] 3d⁶ 4s², so it is a transition element.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Which element has the highest first ionisation enthalpy?
questions.explanation: Helium's electrons are very close to the nucleus and in a complete shell, so it has the highest first ionisation enthalpy of all elements.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: An element X has atomic number 17. Which element will be most similar to X in chemical properties?
questions.explanation: Atomic number 17 is chlorine (Group 17); atomic number 9 is fluorine, in the same group.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Among the following elements of the third period, which is the strongest reducing agent?
questions.explanation: Sodium loses its single outer electron most easily, so it is the strongest reducing agent.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Why does a Group 1 element have a lower ionisation enthalpy than the Group 2 element in the same period?
questions.answer: The Group 1 atom has a larger radius and a smaller nuclear charge, and its single ns electron is easier to remove. In the Group 2 atom the nuclear charge is higher, the atom is smaller and its filled ns² subshell is more stable, so more energy is needed.
keyPoints: Group 1 atom is larger with lower nuclear charge
Group 2 has higher nuclear charge and smaller size
questions.explanation: Ionisation enthalpy increases across a period.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: A covalent bond is formed by:
options: sharing of electron pairs between atoms
complete transfer of electrons from one atom to another
attraction between metal ions and a sea of electrons
questions.explanation: In a covalent bond two atoms share one or more pairs of electrons.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: What is an electrovalent (ionic) bond? Explain its formation in sodium chloride.
questions.answer: An ionic bond is the electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions formed by the transfer of electrons. Sodium loses one electron to become Na⁺ and chlorine gains it to become Cl⁻; both then have noble gas configurations and the ions attract each other.
keyPoints: Na becomes Na⁺ and Cl becomes Cl⁻
Electrostatic attraction holds the ions together
questions.explanation: Elements with low ionisation enthalpy and high electron gain enthalpy form ionic bonds.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Which of the following molecules contains a polar covalent bond?
questions.explanation: H and Cl differ in electronegativity, so the shared pair is displaced towards Cl; in Cl₂, N₂ and O₂ the atoms are identical.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: How many sigma (σ) bonds are present in a molecule of ethene, C₂H₄?
questions.explanation: There are four C-H sigma bonds and one C-C sigma bond; the second C-C bond is a pi bond.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: The shape of a BeCl₂ molecule in the gas phase is:
questions.explanation: Be has two bond pairs and no lone pair (sp hybridisation), so the molecule is linear.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Which of the following molecules has a zero dipole moment?
questions.explanation: CCl₄ is a symmetrical tetrahedron, so the four bond dipoles cancel each other.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Which of the following molecules has a bent (angular) shape?
questions.explanation: The sulphur atom in SO₂ has a lone pair as well as two bond pairs, which gives a bent shape; the others are linear or trigonal planar.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Explain why ice floats on liquid water.
questions.answer: In ice the water molecules are held by hydrogen bonds in an open cage-like hexagonal structure with empty spaces. This arrangement makes ice less dense than liquid water, where the molecules are packed closer together, so ice floats.
keyPoints: Hydrogen bonding in ice gives an open structure
Ice has a lower density than liquid water
questions.explanation: This property protects aquatic life in cold regions because ponds freeze from the top.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Which structure forms the outer boundary of an animal cell?
questions.explanation: Animal cells have no cell wall, so the plasma membrane is the outer boundary.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Name two organelles of eukaryotic cells that are bounded by a double membrane.
questions.answer: The mitochondrion and the chloroplast (a plastid) are double-membrane organelles. The nucleus also has a double membrane, the nuclear envelope.
questions.explanation: Mitochondria and chloroplasts are believed to have evolved from engulfed prokaryotes.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Which organelle is mainly responsible for the synthesis of lipids in the cell?
questions.explanation: The smooth ER makes lipids and steroids.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Chromatin in the nucleus is made of:
questions.explanation: Chromatin is DNA wrapped around histone proteins, with some RNA.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Starch is stored in plant cells in plastids called:
questions.explanation: Amyloplasts are colourless plastids that store starch; elaioplasts store oils and fats.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: An animal cell is placed in a solution that is more concentrated than its cytoplasm. The cell will:
questions.explanation: Water moves out of the cell by osmosis towards the more concentrated solution, so the cell shrinks.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: A cell cannot grow indefinitely large mainly because, as a cell grows:
options: its surface area increases faster than its volume
its volume increases faster than its surface area, making exchange with surroundings less efficient
questions.explanation: Volume grows with the cube of size and surface area with the square, so the surface area per unit volume falls and exchange of materials becomes inadequate.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: What would be the effect on a cell if its nucleolus were damaged?
questions.answer: The nucleolus is the site where ribosomal RNA is made and ribosome subunits are assembled. If it is damaged, new ribosomes cannot be formed properly, so protein synthesis in the cell would be affected.
keyPoints: Nucleolus makes rRNA and assembles ribosome subunits
questions.explanation: Cells that make a lot of protein have prominent nucleoli.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: The most abundant protein in the animal world is:
questions.explanation: Collagen, found in skin, bone and connective tissue, is the most abundant protein in animals.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: What are enzymes? Give two examples.
questions.answer: Enzymes are biological catalysts, mostly proteins, that speed up chemical reactions in living organisms without being used up. Examples: amylase, pepsin, catalase.
keyPoints: Speed up reactions without being consumed
questions.explanation: Each enzyme acts on a specific substrate.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: A molecule of fat (triglyceride) is formed from glycerol and:
questions.explanation: One glycerol molecule is joined to three fatty acids by ester bonds.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Which sugar is present in RNA?
questions.explanation: RNA stands for ribonucleic acid; its sugar is ribose.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Two monosaccharides are joined together in a disaccharide by a:
questions.explanation: A glycosidic bond forms between two sugar units with the loss of a water molecule.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: The enzyme pepsin works best in the stomach because its optimum pH is:
questions.explanation: Pepsin is adapted to the highly acidic gastric juice.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: In an enzyme-catalysed reaction, the rate stops rising when the substrate concentration is increased far above a certain value because:
options: the enzyme is destroyed by the substrate
all the active sites of the enzyme molecules are occupied
questions.explanation: At saturation every enzyme molecule is working at its maximum rate, so more substrate cannot speed it up.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: What are essential amino acids? Why must they be supplied in the diet?
questions.answer: Essential amino acids are those that the human body cannot synthesise in sufficient amounts, so they must be obtained from food. Without them the body cannot make all the proteins it needs.
questions.explanation: Examples include leucine, lysine and tryptophan.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Leaves look green because chlorophyll:
options: makes a green pigment from soil minerals
is green because of the water in leaves
absorbs mainly red and blue light and reflects green light
questions.explanation: Chlorophyll absorbs red and blue wavelengths and the green light that is reflected or transmitted reaches our eyes.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Name the site of the Calvin cycle in a chloroplast and the two products of the light reactions that it uses.
questions.answer: The Calvin cycle occurs in the stroma of the chloroplast. It uses ATP and NADPH produced in the light reactions.
questions.explanation: These supply the energy and reducing power to fix CO₂ into sugar.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Most of the ATP in aerobic respiration is produced in the:
questions.explanation: The electron transport chain on the inner mitochondrial membrane produces the bulk of the ATP.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: When yeast ferments glucose in the absence of oxygen, the products are:
questions.explanation: Yeast converts pyruvic acid into ethanol and CO₂ in alcoholic fermentation.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: The splitting of water in the light reactions (photolysis) is associated with:
questions.explanation: The oxygen-evolving complex of photosystem II splits water to give electrons, protons and oxygen.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Succulent desert plants with Crassulacean acid metabolism (CAM) open their stomata at night mainly to:
options: take in CO₂ while losing less water
questions.explanation: The air is cooler and more humid at night, so less water is lost while CO₂ is fixed and stored for daytime use.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: In Engelmann's experiment, aerobic bacteria collected mainly in the blue and red regions of the spectrum falling on a filament of a green alga because:
options: bacteria need blue and red light to live
the alga is killed in the other regions
photosynthesis, and so oxygen release, was greatest in those regions
questions.explanation: The bacteria move to where oxygen is released most, which shows that blue and red light are most effective for photosynthesis.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: What is photorespiration and why is it considered a wasteful process?
questions.answer: In photorespiration RuBisCO combines RuBP with oxygen instead of CO₂, so carbon is lost as CO₂ without making sugar. It also does not produce ATP or NADPH but uses energy, so it reduces the efficiency of photosynthesis in C₃ plants.
keyPoints: RuBisCO acts on O₂ instead of CO₂
CO₂ is released and no sugar is made
No ATP or NADPH produced; energy is consumed
questions.explanation: C₄ plants avoid most of this loss.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: The voice box in humans is the:
questions.explanation: The larynx contains the vocal cords and helps in sound production.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Name the four main components of human blood.
questions.answer: Plasma, red blood cells (erythrocytes), white blood cells (leucocytes) and platelets (thrombocytes).
questions.explanation: Plasma is the liquid part, about 55% of the blood.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Which blood cells mainly protect the body against infections?
questions.explanation: White blood cells (leucocytes) are the cells of the immune defence.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: The human heart is enclosed in a double-walled protective sac called the:
questions.explanation: The pericardium surrounds the heart and contains a lubricating fluid.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: The haemoglobin content of normal human blood is about:
questions.explanation: A healthy adult has about 12 to 16 g of haemoglobin per 100 mL of blood.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: The respiratory rhythm centre in the medulla is most sensitive to changes in the blood level of:
questions.explanation: A rise in CO₂ and H⁺ stimulates the centre to increase the rate and depth of breathing.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Human blood circulation is called 'double circulation' because:
options: blood passes through the heart twice in one complete circuit of the body
blood flows in both directions in the same vessel
questions.explanation: Blood goes from heart to lungs and back to the heart (pulmonary circuit), and then from heart to body and back (systemic circuit).

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Why does the narrowing of arteries by fatty deposits (atherosclerosis) tend to raise blood pressure?
questions.answer: Deposits such as cholesterol plaques narrow the lumen of the arteries and make them less elastic, so there is more resistance to blood flow. The heart has to pump harder to push the blood through, so the pressure rises.
keyPoints: Heart pumps harder, so blood pressure increases
questions.explanation: Pressure depends on the cardiac output and the resistance in the vessels.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: What is the SI unit of frequency?
questions.explanation: Frequency is the number of cycles per second and is measured in hertz (Hz).

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Which instrument should be used to measure the diameter of a thin wire to the nearest 0.01 mm?
options: Vernier calliper with least count 0.1 mm
questions.explanation: A screw gauge typically has a least count of 0.01 mm, suitable for thin wires.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: What is the SI unit of electric current?
questions.explanation: The ampere (A) is the SI base unit of electric current.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: One nanometre (1 nm) is equal to:
questions.explanation: The prefix nano means 10⁻⁹.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: What is the dimensional formula of frequency?
questions.explanation: Frequency is the reciprocal of time period, so its dimension is T⁻¹.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Masses of 12.11 g, 18.0 g and 1.013 g are added. Report the sum to the correct number of significant figures.
questions.answer: The raw sum is 31.123 g. The least precise value (18.0 g) has one decimal place, so the result is rounded to 31.1 g.
keyPoints: Limited by the value with fewest decimal places (18.0)
questions.explanation: In addition, the answer cannot be more precise than the least precise term.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: For a spring-mass system, the expression √(m/k) is used, where m is mass and k is the spring constant (force per unit extension). Its dimensions are those of:
questions.explanation: k has dimensions MT⁻², so m/k = T², and the square root is T.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Express the speed of light, 3 × 10⁸ m/s, in km/h.
questions.answer: 3 × 10⁸ m/s = 3 × 10⁵ km/s. Multiplying by 3600 s per hour gives 1.08 × 10⁹ km/h.
questions.explanation: Unit conversions use conversion factors consistently.

questions.subject: science
questions.topic: Motion in a Straight Line and in a Plane
questions.q: A ball is thrown horizontally from the top of a tower. Ignoring air resistance, its horizontal velocity during the flight:
questions.explanation: No horizontal force acts, so the horizontal component of velocity does not change.

questions.subject: science
questions.topic: Motion in a Straight Line and in a Plane
questions.q: Which of the following can have a negative value?
questions.explanation: Displacement is a vector and can be negative relative to a chosen direction; distance and speed cannot be negative.

questions.subject: science
questions.topic: Motion in a Straight Line and in a Plane
questions.q: What is the SI unit of angular velocity?
questions.explanation: Angular velocity is angle per unit time, measured in radians per second.

questions.subject: science
questions.topic: Motion in a Straight Line and in a Plane
questions.q: A car travels 60 km in the first hour and 40 km in the second hour along a straight road. What is its average speed?
questions.explanation: Average speed = total distance / total time = 100 / 2 = 50 km/h.

questions.subject: science
questions.topic: Motion in a Straight Line and in a Plane
questions.q: A horizontal straight line at v = 5 m/s on a velocity-time graph represents:
options: motion with uniform velocity and zero acceleration
questions.explanation: The velocity is constant, so the slope (acceleration) is zero.

questions.subject: science
questions.topic: Motion in a Straight Line and in a Plane
questions.q: A stone is thrown horizontally at 10 m/s from the top of a 20 m high cliff. Taking g = 10 m/s², find the time taken to reach the ground and the horizontal distance covered.
questions.answer: Vertical motion: 20 = ½ × 10 × t², so t = 2 s. Horizontal distance = 10 × 2 = 20 m.
questions.explanation: Horizontal and vertical motions are independent.

questions.subject: science
questions.topic: Motion in a Straight Line and in a Plane
questions.q: In uniform circular motion, the angle between the velocity and the acceleration of the body is:
questions.explanation: Velocity is tangential and the acceleration points to the centre, so they are perpendicular.

questions.subject: science
questions.topic: Motion in a Straight Line and in a Plane
questions.q: Two forces of 3 N and 4 N act on a body at right angles to each other. Find the magnitude of the resultant and its direction relative to the 3 N force.
questions.answer: Magnitude = √(3² + 4²) = 5 N. The angle with the 3 N force is tan⁻¹(4/3), about 53°.
keyPoints: Use the Pythagoras theorem for perpendicular vectors
Angle about 53° from the 3 N force
questions.explanation: Vectors at right angles are added using the parallelogram law.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: A card is placed on a glass with a coin on the card. When the card is flicked away sharply, the coin drops into the glass. This demonstrates:
questions.explanation: The coin tends to stay at rest when the card is removed quickly, so it falls straight down.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: The same force acts on a small car and on a heavy truck. Which one gets the greater acceleration?
questions.explanation: a = F/m, so the body with the smaller mass has the larger acceleration.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: A 2 kg book lies on a horizontal table. Taking g = 10 m/s², the normal reaction of the table on the book is:
questions.explanation: The book is in equilibrium, so the normal force equals its weight, 2 × 10 = 20 N.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: A 10 kg body on a frictionless horizontal surface is pulled by a horizontal force of 20 N. Its acceleration is:

questions.subject: science
questions.q: The coefficient of static friction between a 5 kg block and a floor is 0.4. Taking g = 10 m/s², the limiting friction is:
questions.explanation: Limiting friction = μN = 0.4 × 50 = 20 N.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: According to Newton's third law, the action and reaction forces are equal and opposite. Why do they not cancel each other?
questions.answer: The action and reaction forces act on two different bodies, not on the same body. Forces cancel only when they act on the same body, so the pair never cancels.
keyPoints: Action and reaction act on different bodies
Cancellation needs forces on the same body
questions.explanation: Each body responds to the force that acts on it.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Blocks of mass 2 kg and 3 kg are in contact on a smooth horizontal surface. A horizontal force of 10 N is applied to the 2 kg block, pushing it against the 3 kg block. What force does the 2 kg block exert on the 3 kg block?
questions.explanation: The common acceleration is 10/5 = 2 m/s², so the force on the 3 kg block is 3 × 2 = 6 N.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: A 5 kg block remains at rest on a rough plane inclined at 30° to the horizontal. Taking g = 10 m/s², find the force of friction on the block.
questions.answer: The block is in equilibrium, so friction balances the component of weight along the incline: f = mg sin 30° = 5 × 10 × 0.5 = 25 N, directed up the incline.
questions.explanation: Static friction adjusts to the force needed to hold the block.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Work is a:
questions.explanation: Work is the scalar product of force and displacement.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: The gravitational potential energy of a body near the Earth's surface depends on its:
questions.explanation: PE = mgh depends on the height.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: One joule is equal to how many ergs?
questions.explanation: 1 J = 10⁷ erg.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: A spring of force constant 100 N/m is stretched by 0.2 m. The energy stored in it is:

questions.subject: science
questions.q: A 2 kg body falls through 5 m under gravity (g = 10 m/s²). The work done by gravity is:
questions.explanation: W = mgh = 2 × 10 × 5 = 100 J, positive since the force and displacement are in the same direction.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Differentiate between kinetic energy and potential energy, with one example of each.
questions.answer: Kinetic energy is the energy a body has because of its motion (a moving car). Potential energy is the energy a body has because of its position or configuration (water in a raised tank, a stretched spring).
keyPoints: Potential: due to position or configuration
questions.explanation: Both are mechanical energy and can be converted into each other.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Two bodies of masses m and 4m have the same kinetic energy. What is the ratio of their momenta?
questions.explanation: p = √(2mK), so the ratio is √m : √(4m) = 1 : 2.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: A 1000 kg car moving at 20 m/s is stopped by a constant braking force of 4000 N. Find the stopping distance.
questions.answer: KE = ½ × 1000 × 20² = 200000 J. Work done by the brakes F × d must equal this, so d = 200000 / 4000 = 50 m.
questions.explanation: The work-energy theorem links the braking work to the loss of kinetic energy.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Weight is measured in:
questions.explanation: Weight is a force, so its SI unit is the newton.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: The Moon is a natural satellite of:
questions.explanation: The Moon orbits the Earth.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: According to Kepler's laws, a planet that is farther from the Sun has a:
questions.explanation: T² is proportional to a³, so a larger orbit means a longer period.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: As a body is taken from the Earth's surface to a height above it, the acceleration due to gravity:
questions.explanation: g = GM/r² falls as the distance r from the centre increases.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Taking g on the Moon as 1.6 m/s², the weight of a 60 kg astronaut there is:

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Define orbital velocity and write its expression for a satellite in a circular orbit of radius r around a planet of mass M.
questions.answer: Orbital velocity is the speed a satellite must have to stay in a circular orbit. Gravity provides the centripetal force, so GMm/r² = mv²/r, giving v = √(GM/r).
keyPoints: Speed needed to remain in orbit
questions.explanation: It is independent of the satellite's mass.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: The ratio of the escape velocity to the orbital velocity of a satellite moving very close to the Earth's surface is:
questions.explanation: v_escape = √(2gR) and v_orbital = √(gR), so the ratio is √2.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: A planet has one-tenth the mass of the Earth and half its radius. Find the acceleration due to gravity at its surface in terms of g on Earth.
questions.answer: g' = G(M/10)/(R/2)² = (4/10) GM/R² = 0.4 g, which is about 3.9 m/s².
keyPoints: g is proportional to M / R²
questions.explanation: Halving the radius multiplies g by 4 and one-tenth mass divides it by 10.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Which of the following is a compound?
questions.explanation: Water consists of two elements, hydrogen and oxygen, chemically combined.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: The chemical symbol of potassium is:
questions.explanation: The symbol K comes from its Latin name kalium.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: What is the molecular mass of sulphuric acid, H₂SO₄? (H = 1, S = 32, O = 16)

questions.subject: science
questions.q: How many atoms are present in 1 mole of water molecules? (N_A = 6.022 × 10²³)
questions.explanation: Each molecule has 3 atoms, so 3 × 6.022 × 10²³ ≈ 1.8 × 10²⁴ atoms.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: What is the mass of 0.25 mol of NaOH? (Na = 23, O = 16, H = 1)

questions.subject: science
questions.q: State Gay-Lussac's law of gaseous volumes with an example.
questions.answer: When gases react, they do so in volumes that bear a simple whole-number ratio to one another and to the volumes of gaseous products, at the same temperature and pressure. Example: 2 volumes of hydrogen react with 1 volume of oxygen to give 2 volumes of steam.
keyPoints: Example: 2 : 1 : 2 for H₂, O₂ and steam
questions.explanation: Avogadro's law later explained this observation.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: What is the percentage of oxygen by mass in water, H₂O? (H = 1, O = 16)

questions.subject: science
questions.q: What mass of oxygen is needed to burn 4 g of hydrogen completely? 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O (H = 1, O = 16)
questions.answer: 4 g of H₂ is 2 mol. By the equation 2 mol of H₂ needs 1 mol of O₂, which is 32 g.
questions.explanation: The mole ratio from the balanced equation links the amounts.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Cathode rays are streams of:
questions.explanation: Thomson showed that cathode rays consist of negatively charged electrons.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: What is the electric charge on a neutron?
questions.explanation: A neutron is electrically neutral.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: The mass of a proton is approximately how many times the mass of an electron?
questions.explanation: A proton is about 1836 times as massive as an electron.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: How many electrons are there in the outermost shell of an oxygen atom (atomic number 8)?
questions.explanation: The configuration 1s² 2s² 2p⁴ has 6 electrons in the second shell.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: An orbital with n = 2 and l = 1 is called:
questions.explanation: l = 1 corresponds to a p orbital, and n = 2 gives 2p.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: State Hund's rule of maximum multiplicity and apply it to the 2p electrons of nitrogen.
questions.answer: Electrons occupy the orbitals of a subshell singly with parallel spins before any orbital is filled with a second electron. In nitrogen (2p³) the three p electrons occupy the three p orbitals separately with parallel spins.
keyPoints: Pairing does not start until every orbital has one electron
questions.explanation: This arrangement lowers the energy through reduced repulsion.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: In a multi-electron atom, which of the orbitals 3d, 4s, 4p and 4d has the highest energy (using the n + l rule)?
questions.explanation: The n + l values are 5, 4, 5 and 6, so 4d has the highest energy.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Calculate the wavelength of light of frequency 6 × 10¹⁴ Hz. (c = 3 × 10⁸ m/s)
questions.answer: λ = c/ν = 3 × 10⁸ / 6 × 10¹⁴ = 5 × 10⁻⁷ m, which is 500 nm.
questions.explanation: This wavelength is in the green region of visible light.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: How many periods does the modern periodic table have?
questions.explanation: The table has 7 periods (horizontal rows) and 18 groups.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Which of the following is a non-metal that is liquid at room temperature?
questions.explanation: Bromine is a liquid non-metal; mercury is a liquid metal, chlorine is a gas and iodine is a solid.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Oxygen (atomic number 8) belongs to which group of the periodic table?
questions.explanation: Oxygen has six valence electrons (2s² 2p⁴), which places it in Group 16.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Which is larger in size?
questions.explanation: The chloride ion has an extra electron, so the repulsion is greater and the radius is larger.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: An element has the electron arrangement 2, 8, 2. The element is:
questions.explanation: The element has 12 electrons, so its atomic number is 12, which is magnesium.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Why do elements in the same group of the periodic table show similar chemical properties?
questions.answer: Elements in a group have the same number of valence electrons and a similar outer electronic configuration. Chemical properties depend mainly on the valence electrons, so they behave alike.
questions.explanation: Properties vary gradually down the group because of increasing size.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Which of the following sequences shows increasing atomic radius?
questions.explanation: Atomic radius increases down a group as more shells are added.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Why is hydrogen placed in a position by itself in the periodic table rather than clearly in Group 1 or Group 17?
questions.answer: Hydrogen has one electron in its outer shell (1s¹), like the alkali metals, but it is one electron short of the helium configuration, like the halogens. It also exists as a diatomic non-metal gas, so it does not fit neatly into either group.
keyPoints: Needs one electron to complete its shell like halogens
Properties are unique, so it is placed separately
questions.explanation: Its properties are not fully similar to any single group.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Ionic compounds generally have:
questions.explanation: The strong electrostatic attraction between ions in the lattice needs a lot of energy to overcome.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: How many valence electrons does a chlorine atom have?
questions.explanation: Chlorine has the configuration 2, 8, 7, so seven valence electrons.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: The H–C–H bond angle in methane is:
questions.explanation: In a regular tetrahedron the bond angle is 109.5°.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: The nitrogen atom in ammonia (NH₃) is hybridised as:
questions.explanation: Three bond pairs and one lone pair make four electron pairs, which corresponds to sp³ hybridisation.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Which of these species has a tetrahedral shape?
questions.explanation: NH₄⁺ has four bond pairs and no lone pair on nitrogen.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: What is a hydrogen bond? Give one example of a substance in which it occurs.
questions.answer: A hydrogen bond is a weak attraction between a hydrogen atom covalently bonded to a highly electronegative atom (N, O or F) and a lone pair on another electronegative atom. It occurs in water, ammonia and hydrogen fluoride.
keyPoints: H attached to N, O or F
Attraction to a lone pair on a neighbouring molecule
questions.explanation: It is much weaker than a covalent bond but strongly affects boiling points.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Among O₂, O₂⁺ and O₂⁻, which has the shortest bond length?
options: All have the same bond length
questions.explanation: The bond orders are 2 (O₂), 2.5 (O₂⁺) and 1.5 (O₂⁻); the higher the bond order, the shorter the bond.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: The B-F bonds in BF₃ are polar, but BF₃ has zero dipole moment. Explain.
questions.answer: BF₃ is trigonal planar with bond angles of 120°. The three equal B-F bond dipoles are arranged symmetrically and cancel each other, so the net dipole moment is zero.
keyPoints: They cancel, net dipole is zero
questions.explanation: Symmetry can make a molecule non-polar despite polar bonds.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Which of the following organelles is found only in plant cells?
questions.explanation: Chloroplasts carry out photosynthesis and are found in plant cells and algae, not animal cells.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Which structure in a plant cell is a large fluid-filled sac that stores water and dissolved substances?
questions.explanation: The central vacuole stores water, salts and pigments, and helps keep the cell turgid.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Which of the following is absent from a bacterial cell?
questions.explanation: Bacteria are prokaryotes and lack membrane-bound organelles such as mitochondria.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: 70S ribosomes are found in the cytoplasm of:
questions.explanation: Prokaryotic cells have 70S ribosomes; the cytoplasmic ribosomes of eukaryotes are 80S.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Which of the following organelles is NOT bounded by a membrane?
questions.explanation: Ribosomes are made of RNA and protein and have no membrane around them.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Describe briefly the structure of a mitochondrion.
questions.answer: A mitochondrion has a smooth outer membrane and an inner membrane folded into cristae. The space enclosed by the inner membrane is the matrix, which contains enzymes, a circular DNA molecule and ribosomes.
keyPoints: Matrix contains enzymes, DNA and ribosomes
questions.explanation: The cristae increase the surface area for ATP production.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: A red blood cell is placed in an isotonic saline solution. What happens to its size?
questions.explanation: In an isotonic solution there is no net movement of water, so the cell keeps its size.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Why are mitochondria and chloroplasts described as semi-autonomous organelles?
questions.answer: Each contains its own DNA and ribosomes and can make some of its own proteins and divide independently. But they still depend on the nucleus for many of their proteins, so they are only partly independent.
keyPoints: Have their own DNA and ribosomes
Make some of their own proteins and divide
Depend on nuclear genes for the rest
questions.explanation: This supports the idea that they evolved from free-living prokaryotes.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: The exoskeleton of insects contains the polysaccharide:
questions.explanation: Chitin is a nitrogen-containing polysaccharide present in arthropod exoskeletons and fungal cell walls.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Lipids are generally insoluble in:
questions.explanation: Lipids are non-polar and dissolve in organic solvents but not in water.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: How many different amino acids are commonly found in proteins?
questions.explanation: Twenty standard amino acids are used to build proteins.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Which type of RNA carries amino acids to the ribosome during protein synthesis?
questions.explanation: Transfer RNA (tRNA) brings amino acids to the ribosome.
